quoted_text:
Huge massive news!!!

Breaking: UK-regulated crypto exchanges (qualifying cryptoasset trading platforms, or QCATPs) will be barred from acting as market makers on their own platforms!!

What the rules actually say
•  HM Treasury made amending regulations on 18 November 2026 (SI 2026/1219) that add Article 9UA to the framework. This excludes “market making on a qualifying cryptoasset trading platform” from the regulated activity of dealing in qualifying cryptoassets as principal (Article 9T). 

•  FCA final rules (including in CRYPTO 6) explicitly state that a firm cannot act as a market maker on a UK QCATP it operates. The operator must stay neutral. 

•  Independent third-party firms (or separate affiliates under non-discriminatory access rules) can make markets on those platforms without needing principal-dealing permission for that activity. 

This covers spot Bitcoin and other qualifying cryptoassets.

•  Operators can still do matched-principal execution of client orders (interposing themselves between buyer and seller with no market risk and simultaneous matching) if they have the extra permission and follow non-discretionary venue rules. Pure proprietary market-making on their own book is off-limits.

Why this matters

The aim is to reduce conflicts of interest and stop exchanges from trading against their own customers with an informational or operational advantage. Exchanges must identify, monitor, and disclose market-making arrangements and any incentives they offer to liquidity providers.

Existing UK crypto firms that want transitional protection under the new full FSMA regime must apply for the relevant permissions by 28 February 2027. The new regime itself goes live on 25 October 2027.
In short: the exchange runs the venue; independent market makers provide the liquidity. The operator is not allowed to be both referee and player on its own pitch.

i think you get a lot of japanese soldiers sitting in the middle of that chasm (both builders or investors) who will still believe otherwise, or believe it was a failure of the builders [which don't get me wrong, is true to the 95th degree] and that if the right honest builder comes along, everything will be solved and the key to the problem will be unlocked. it's just not true unfortunately; the problem is that gaming in its traditional form factor is basically not isomorphic to any succeeding crypto category and it largely does not benefit from crypto.

there are of course some ideas which are fun for an extremely niche subset of nerds like us on the internet (like 'autonomous worlds' and other bottom-up game designs) but these aren't conducive to producing something that can (a) produce value for holders and (b) actually have potential to scale exponentially once capital is injected into it. they would be fun problems to solve and we've had plenty of concepts over the years, but they just don't have a real end game that goes beyond a short term pump and dump.

this is what we mean by fitting what we are doing into the new age: there is no point in pursuing something that we know for a fact is going to be a dead end -- and that is every single direction right now which exists in crypto outside of the two ends of the barbells i've discussed.

from the outside i know the conclusion from most people is that "they are just building a game and a brand, what's so hard about that? why is it taking so long? why do comms suck?" but the problem set and chain of decisions is much wider than that. 

realistically it's the following:
- where is crypto going
- what are we & what do we have that exists so far
- how do we package all of what we have built so far and then isomorphically force it into a societal trend that actually has PMF
- is there a business model here with that repackaging which can scale exponentially and create economic value for holders [that goes beyond just being "a cool fun thing to play with"]
- can this business model / product also benefit from having the same persona-type of our pre-exisitng community (i.e. does it make sense for us to, and do we get an advantage from, building a prediction market or a perp dex, prob not)

this is a really, retardly hard problem when you're not working from a fresh slate and you have a community with a set of expectations...one of my biggest failures has probably been not trusting my instincts and hard pivoting towards things i know would work out, rather than trying to do that whilst upholding pre-existing expectations -- this should explain the silence and why we've just been more fixated internally on really angling towards product ideas what we know have a good chance of succeeding and working at scale. as opposed to just releasing things as they are, coasting and then hitting people with an "oops sorry didn't work out" as we knew they would, because the category itself has been invalidated.

and to add on here, since we were using AI pretty early on (practically since the beginning of the company, when i was a bit more of a doubter and diakou was telling me i was coping and to stfu) we've had a lot of foresight of this, and it has almost felt retarded to row our boat down a river path knowing there is going to be a waterfall at the end. between knowing the natural ending point of where AI takes us, and capitalism reaching its end game. i think me, diakou, et al, have a really hard time going for small wins when we know the direction is totally off and they don't successively chain into something bigger. this is why likely to you it looks like we're spotty with shipping & communication when it's moreso just making sure we don't self-induce more baggage that may have to be pivoted away from once we find the thing that has PMF for us -- for example, we had some big adjacent wins with things like Roblox yet we still get dragged for it to this day with people claiming it does nothing for holders and just lines our pockets (?).

whether people see it as self-induced stasis, a skill issue of the team, a failure of wab, or whatever else is largely irrelevant to me, and i understand the above can read as me just giving excuses. i'm just trying to be as honest as possible so you and others can understand where we were at, where we are at, and how exactly we're navigating it towards an end game. hopefully that explained some of the context from early on till now outside of all of the other hiccups you're already aware of.

and on that note with some good news; i think we've found a way to package and squeeze absolutely everything we've done into a form factor that we believe crypto users and normies alike will both enjoy, and that can be scaled if we get the unit economics down behind it. our model is not too dissimilar to others which have found some small successes in crypto [and there are some competitors in web2 which have found PMF with a somewhat similar product], and part of the model is also isomorphic to one of the categories that actually has PMF in crypto. a little bit frankenstein-y but i don't think it has been truly attempted before and could carve out a niche.

i won't elaborate more as to not drive your expectations up and disappoint, but i will say it's more true to our original vision we set out to have, and having access to compute has made it a lot easier for us to fulfill. and tbh, i've been having much more fun these past few months than the past couple years so that should be an indicator of the enthusiasm and momentum we've had towards building this all out.

if/when we do succeed in this, we will be like japanese soldiers that stayed in the jungle but somehow survived through WW3 after surviving WW2. arf arf

text:
Huge massive news!!!

Breaking: UK-regulated crypto exchanges (qualifying cryptoasset trading platforms, or QCATPs) will be barred from acting as market makers on their own platforms!!

What the rules actually say
•  HM Treasury made amending regulations on 18 November 2026 (SI 2026/1219) that add Article 9UA to the framework. This excludes “market making on a qualifying cryptoasset trading platform” from the regulated activity of dealing in qualifying cryptoassets as principal (Article 9T). 

•  FCA final rules (including in CRYPTO 6) explicitly state that a firm cannot act as a market maker on a UK QCATP it operates. The operator must stay neutral. 

•  Independent third-party firms (or separate affiliates under non-discriminatory access rules) can make markets on those platforms without needing principal-dealing permission for that activity. 

This covers spot Bitcoin and other qualifying cryptoassets.

•  Operators can still do matched-principal execution of client orders (interposing themselves between buyer and seller with no market risk and simultaneous matching) if they have the extra permission and follow non-discretionary venue rules. Pure proprietary market-making on their own book is off-limits.

Why this matters

The aim is to reduce conflicts of interest and stop exchanges from trading against their own customers with an informational or operational advantage. Exchanges must identify, monitor, and disclose market-making arrangements and any incentives they offer to liquidity providers.

Existing UK crypto firms that want transitional protection under the new full FSMA regime must apply for the relevant permissions by 28 February 2027. The new regime itself goes live on 25 October 2027.
In short: the exchange runs the venue; independent market makers provide the liquidity. The operator is not allowed to be both referee and player on its own pitch.

text:
In the early 1970s, the ideology of the left began capturing every institution in the West.

And today we live in a world that's burning because of it.

This was no accident. It was a strategy. And it has a name.

In the early 1930s, from his prison cell, Antonio Gramsci understood something Lenin never did: in the West, you don't take power through factories or guns. You take it through culture. Control the schools, the universities, the press and the artists, and political power will eventually fall into your hands on its own. He called it cultural hegemony.

In France, the door was opened by the man you'd least expect: de Gaulle.

In 1944, to disarm the communist militias and restore order, he pardoned Maurice Thorez, freshly back from Moscow, and brought communist ministers into the government. The Communist Party became the largest party in France. The unspoken postwar deal was simple: the State, the army and the economy for the Gaullists. Ideas, schools and culture for the left.

De Gaulle thought power meant the State. Gramsci knew it meant culture.

May 68 sent the bill. The General won the June elections in a landslide, then his government handed the 68ers their very own university: Vincennes. Foucault ran the philosophy department. Deleuze, Lyotard and Badiou taught there.

The 1970s did the rest. Foucault, Derrida, Deleuze, Bourdieu. French Theory crossed the Atlantic and moved into American campuses. The project: deconstruct everything. The nation, the family, merit, truth itself. Everything became a power relation. If you succeed, you're an oppressor. If you fail, you're a victim.

Fifty years later, the long march through the institutions is complete.

The result is a piece of software. Installed across the entire West. Schools, universities, media, and above all culture: artists, actors, singers, athletes. The vast majority of people with an audience run on the same OS. And those who don't have learned to keep quiet.

I talk about this a lot with people inside that system. In private, many of them think the exact opposite of what they say in public. But they know one wrong sentence means the end of the roles, the contracts, the invitations.

So yes, a lot of artists end up selling their soul to the devil.

Not the conspiracy theorists' devil, with symbols and rituals. A far more ordinary one: leftist conformity. You repeat the talking points, you sign the right open letter at the right moment, and you keep your career.

And that software is a total lie.

It promised equality and delivered stagnation. It promised liberation and delivered censorship. It promised social peace and fractured every society it touched.

Today, it's dying everywhere. Not because we fought it. Because it's hitting its limits. Reality always sends the bill.

I believe 1970 to 2030 will be remembered as the West's cultural dark age. Sixty years of telling the most creative civilization in history that it should be ashamed of itself.

And I believe a renaissance comes right after.

Renaissances never come from institutions. They come from people who build outside them. And for the first time, with AI, anyone can create without asking permission from those who guarded the gates.

The software is crashing.

The next one, we write ourselves.

这两天 T3 Code 突然火了，原因很简单

Gemini 4 好评如潮，订阅却被锁死在难用的 Antigravity 里。大家用反代绕过去，结果 magpie 这类项目第二天就被整批封号。

后来 Google 在官方论坛明确表态：只要运行官方原版 antigravity-acp、走它自带的登录，用于个人交互式开发，就是合规的。T3 Code 正是这么做的。

总结了下T3 的优势：

1、合法：别人走反代赌封号，它走官方通道，不用赌

2、不转卖 token：不额外收费，直接用你已有的 Claude / Codex / ChatGPT / Gemini 订阅

3、一个界面管所有 agent：Claude Code、Codex、Cursor、OpenCode、Antigravity 等全支持，对话中途还能切模型，让 Claude 把任务交接给 Codex

4、多端同步：桌面、网页、手机共享同一批 thread，手机上就能批准命令，人不在电脑前 agent 也能继续干活

5、内建 Git：每条 thread 独立 worktree，看 diff、commit、push、开 PR 一键完成

6、扩展快：基于 ACP 架构，新 agent 写个 adapter 就能接入，Gemini 4 一发布就跟上了

7、MIT 开源：约 7 万 star，代码和会话都在本地

适合：手上有多个 agent 订阅、想统一调度、需要用手机远程推进任务的人。

text:
Rahm. Mercy.

Where does it sit in the way we govern?

Cruelty does not always require malice. It can emerge from decisions made at a distance, rules applied without regard for their consequences, or responsibility divided so thoroughly that nobody feels answerable for the person experiencing the result.

Government, law and property rights should help make human life more secure and dignified. When preserving an arrangement takes priority over the lives it affects, we should be willing to examine what that arrangement is now serving.

Mercy belongs in how rules are written, how power is exercised and how mistakes are corrected. It belongs in ordinary administration, in the treatment of vulnerability, in the willingness to understand what a decision will actually ask another person to endure.

A humane system needs consistent rules, proportionate decisions and meaningful ways to challenge harm.

A person should not have to become an exceptional case before their suffering matters.

text:
AI race dynamics are hard to escape when each lab writes its own safety cases and sets its own guardrails for developing more capable models.

We want frontier labs to operate under *common* limits, backed by *shared* safety cases. But the problem is we don't have a good, future-proof yardstick for AI progress that stays useful as models improve.

So we're calling on frontier AI labs to disclose the key metrics they use to track progress, and we propose perplexity as one candidate. We're taking a first step by publishing our own perplexity results over the past five years.

This is scary for us because we've long treated these numbers as sensitive IP. And we know there's still work (perhaps by 3P evaluators) to measure perplexities over the same datasets. But we hope this encourages a norm of sharing key metrics that we can build common safety cases on.

text:
This weekend, I interviewed a couple high school students for MIT. 

I’ve done this every year for almost a decade now. 

And every year, regardless of the state of the world (Covid, AI, War, etc.), I’m reminded that there are still brilliant, hardworking students who want to solve the world’s problems. 

One thing that hasn’t changed through the years, is one piece of advice I give: dream bigger.  

Most MIT students don’t realize the massive set of opportunities they have until after they leave. Your four years at MIT give you every possible opportunity to explore, and while there are plenty of opportunities after you graduate, the potential to explore is lower. 

So when I ask students, “What’s your dream in 20 years?” I’m looking for the most outlandish, crazy goals and desires. 

If you have big dreams, you’ll have the opportunity to go after them at MIT. These are the students who will take advantage of the opportunities given to them. 

Dream bigger.

text:
省流总结一下 OpenAI 首席科学家关于为什么预训练 Scaling 仍然关键的观点。

大前提还是，压缩能力本身可以作为模型智能的一个 proxy。因为想要更高效地压缩未知数据，模型就需要从数据中提炼出更深层、更通用的规律。

有意思的是，OpenAI 长期追踪的 PPL，是在他们内部 codebase 中专门 hold out 的数据上测的。这就意味着两件事：

第一，这部分数据模型在训练时没见过，因此可以用来衡量模型对未知数据的泛化压缩能力。

第二，OpenAI 的 internal codebase 很可能包含大量他们自己 AI research & development 相关的代码。如果是这样，那么模型在这套数据上的压缩能力越强，本身也就越可能具备更强的 AI 研发基础能力，进一步可能转化成参与自身迭代，也就是 RSI 的能力。如果其中还包含 AI for Science 的相关研究代码，那这个指标可能也在一定程度上反映模型进行科学发现的潜在能力。

另外，他还解释了一个很有意思的问题：为什么看起来只有 0.02 的 Loss 优化，也可能对应模型能力上的巨大突破？

因为 Loss 本身存在一个由数据固有熵决定的理论下限，这个下限不会是 0。假设当前模型距离这个下限只剩 0.04，那么再优化 0.02，就相当于把剩余可优化空间直接压缩了 50%。

所以越接近理论下限，看起来越小的 Loss improvement，背后可能对应着越大的智能提升。

从这个角度来看，预训练 Scaling 仍然有很大的空间去不断解锁新的能力，尤其当模型开始能够反过来改进预训练算法时，这个过程甚至可能进一步加速。

quoted_text:
I just built the world's fastest SAT-solver (and it's not even close), thanks to Neon.

Fifteen years ago I spent five years (thousands of hours) working on an advanced Boolean circuit preimage solver, aka a SAT-solver. Building an algorithm to efficiently solve a large subset of the NP-complete problem space in polynomial time is extremely difficult. My solver worked, but it was very slow compared to the state of the art.

Today I gave Neon all my 15-year-old solver code. It analyzed all of the code, took all my best unique ideas and suggested how to improve them using other algorithms, and then it built a highly efficient hybrid solver out of all of the ideas. The result was FAST: MUCH faster than what I had built.

This whole process took LESS THAN FIVE MINUTES. I spent FIVE YEARS in the muddy trenches of number theory and cryptography, and I only got 5% of of the way to where Neon got within 5 minutes.

I gave Neon a handful of ideas as to how to improve its initial algorithm, and two minutes later the solver was 50x faster. I gave it more ideas: 10x faster again. More ideas: 100x faster again.

This new solver, Frobenius, is an alien speed demon. I'm only 20 prompts deep, and Frobenius is already the fastest SAT solver in the world, by a large margin. Frobenius is an average of thousands of times faster than state of the art solvers across all problems, but the gap grows even wider as the problem size increases.🤯

This is how all future progress will be made: through human ⇄ AI symbiotic feedback cycles. We are now cyborgs: augmented human-AI-hybrids. And a human plus an AI will always accomplish more than either individually.

I can't help but think how much more impact I could have had during my career if I had these LLM tools 20+ years ago.

P.S. 1: I'm not ready to release Frobenius yet, because the big SAT solver competition is in April 😁)

P.S. 2: Anthropic is in trouble. Neon is 10x more powerful and 100x faster for hard tasks like this than Opus 5.5. I just canceled three out of my four Claude Ultra plans.

text:
향후 6-9개월 AI 산업에 대한 예측(HiCagr)

AI 경쟁이 더 치열해지면서 막대한 자본이 인프라로 몰리고, 반도체와 핵심 부품 공급사가 가장 큰 수혜를 볼 것

1. 2027년은 AI 학습 경쟁의 해
- 뒤처질 수 없는 게임이라 어떤 AI 랩도 투자를 멈추지 못함
- 앤트로픽은 IPO 자금으로 GW급 컴퓨팅 계약을 맺고, 오픈AI·구글도 60일 안에 맞대응
- 4대 하이퍼스케일러의 2027년 capex 가이던스 합계는 1조 달러 이상

2. 엔비디아 독점 약화
- 구글·아마존 등은 자체 AI 칩(ASIC) 개발을 가속
- 하지만 ASIC과 GPU 모두 TSMC CoWoS, HBM, 광통신 부품이 필요
- 엔비디아의 가격결정력은 약해지고 핵심 공급망의 협상력은 커질 것

3. HBM·DRAM 강세, NAND 약세
- HBM·DRAM은 공급 규율이 유지되지만 NAND 계약가는 2Q27까지 QoQ 하락
- AI 랩들은 메모리 부담 때문에 토큰당 메모리 사용량을 절반 이하로 줄임
- 절감분은 더 긴 컨텍스트와 더 많은 에이전트에 재투입되고, 가격 영향은 2028년 LTA에 반영

4. 다음 병목은 광통신과 전력
- 1.6T 전환이 본격화되면서 고속 레이저, DSP, 실리콘 포토닉스 수요 급증
- HVLP 동박과 T-Glass 공급 부족 지속
- 데이터센터 신규 건설 규제로 이미 전력이 확보된 데이터센터의 가치가 상승

5. AI 사용료는 떨어져도 인프라 수요는 증가
- 최첨단 모델의 토큰당 가격은 50% 이상 하락
- 저렴해진 AI가 더 많은 추론과 에이전트 작업을 유발
- 효율이 좋아질수록 전체 컴퓨팅 수요는 오히려 커지는 구조

6. 결국 반도체가 빅테크보다 유리
- 고금리와 capex 부담에 자금력이 약한 네오클라우드는 최소 1곳이 구조조정 또는 매각
- HBM, ASIC, 첨단 패키징, 광통신 공급사는 AI 경쟁이 이어지는 한 수요 확보
- 2027년 8월 말까지 반도체지수(SOX)가 4대 하이퍼스케일러 수익률을 앞설 것

text:
Breakpoint 2026 (better late than never)

This was my fourth breakpoint, but my first on the  Foundation side, and it was an absolute whirlwind.

What makes us Solana truly special is everyone’s willingness to spark the right connections. Folks are generous with their time, and you aren’t likely to stand in a circle chatting with people without getting introduced to somebody new. Those quick connections turn into group chats that spiral into dinner that turn into lifelong friends, and Breakpoint always feels like the family reunion that jumpstarts it all.

Spent the last 20 days in London immersed in the Solana ecosystem, it’s always an honor to experience it firsthand, or share it with someone new.

Welcoming more than 100 builders into hacker house on Day 1 (a packed house after Halloween) with Events Queen @platis_e, and seeing the sparks of 1000+ people immediately speedrunning cool new Solana products, some from people who had never coded before or opened a wallet.

Organizing more than 35 workshops and 36 demos with the fearless @SuperteamUK (who didn’t have to convince me on the london weather). Shoutout @BlastCtrl who also put together a full mindshare summit inside!

Holding a few (outdoor) Breakpoint sprint meetings to make sure we could best showcase the fire agenda @amiravalliani was cooking on the content side.

Waking up each morning of Hacker House to find an old friend had arrived in town, from coworkers to Superteam Leads to folks I met in an NFT discord along the way.

Celebrating some rush-to-the-finish-line launches ahead of breakpoint with ecosystem teams. There was a point where we were tracking 200+ separate potential announcements 😂

Being a proud theatre mom as the Ecosystem Call and Community Awards productions both went smoothly, and celebrated the big and small wins of the community.

Stepping through the London tube to our Events Team’s magical recreation of Hyde Park and Burroughs Block, to a jam-packed mainstage with every major payments giant on Day 1, and a tour through all of Solana’s best assets on Day 2. Walking through hundreds of ecosystem activations, followed by side events galore, from old favorites (liquidity after dark) to new formats like @joinfrontier or @solflare.

Watching our clipping team and @niran7 crush it on coverage, and @meganenright_ organize dozens of live media productions across the venue. Plus a new @superteam media spotlight to capture new teams (busiest corner of the conference!)

Meeting thousands of builders from every section of Solana, all at different stages of their journey (and wrangling a few last minute product launches that were absolutely worth it!), plus getting the chance to share a drink with coworkers who I’ve only met online.

I could list a hundred more, but what’s the one that stood out to you?

text:
Agent 说“验证完了”，怎么才能真的信它？

很多朋友都被 Agent 坑过：它信誓旦旦说做好了、验证完了，你信以为真，上线后发现压根没做好。被老板骂完回头找它，它认错态度很好，下次还是一样。

问题出在我们让它验证的方式上：Agent 不知道什么叫“做好了”，你也没有低成本的办法确认它真的做好了。分享五条我在用 Agent 做验证时的经验。

一、不要依赖对抗式验证

对抗式验证就是让另一个甚至多个 Agent 来检查结果，执行的 Agent 根据反馈改进，再检查、再改进，直到完成为止。

听起来很好，实际上经常无法收敛。尤其是不太聪明的模型，大部分时候是越改越糟，还浪费了很多 Token。

原因是缺少统一的验收标准。负责检查的 Agent 并不一定知道完整的上下文，也不知道准确的验收标准，于是自作主张提一堆意见，执行的 Agent 再照单全收，结果就越改越偏。

二、给出清晰的验收标准，再给一个能验收的环境

举个例子，你把设计稿交给 Agent，说：“帮我把这几个设计稿做成页面”，通常它会给你一个差不多的结果，有时候出入还很大。

换一个说法：“帮我把这几个设计稿做成页面，完成后请对网页截图，对比设计稿，要求像素一个都不要差”。这时候 Agent 做完不会轻易交差，它会截图，写工具对比截图和设计稿的像素差异，返工重做，直到像素真的一个都不差。

大部分时候我们并不需要一个像素都不差，有些偏差可以接受。重点是让它知道验收标准是什么，并且手里有办法自己去验。

三、越早验证，返工成本越低

尽早验证在传统软件工程里是常识，是大量血泪教训换来的。只是现在 Vibe Coding 让生成代码的成本大幅降低，非专业人士越来越多，大家渐渐忘了写代码之前还有三道关：

可行性分析：这个项目真的值得做吗？做出来会有人用吗？投入产出比合算吗？

原型开发：先做基本的交互，用模拟数据低成本做出一个可运行的原型，快速验证方向对不对，不对马上调整。现在 Agent 做原型已经很强了，比如 Claude Design（或者本地版的 https://t.co/QVpnqsxzMD），做出来的东西和最终结果看起来没什么差别，成本低得多，速度也快。

系统设计：技术选型、模块划分、数据结构、数据库设计、API Schema 这些。设计没做好，系统也能跑，但将来维护成本要高不少。Agent 能力虽然强，选的技术方案并不总是最好的。动手实现之前，先让它写一份技术方案文档，你大概看看：一方面帮你理解项目是怎么实现的，另一方面能及时纠正潜在问题，避免做完再返工。

四、让 Agent 提供证据，降低你的验收成本

人在 Loop 里是必不可少的，完全交给 AI，大概率只能收获 AI Slop。但人的验收能力是瓶颈，要确认的东西太多会很累。我最近用 Antigravity，跨 Workspace 每读一个文件都要我手工确认一遍，简直快崩溃了。

所以要把人确认的成本降到最低：能快速判断结果对不对，快速指出哪里有问题。

最简单的方式，是让 Agent 提供截图、录屏、可视化的 HTML 报告。Agent 在截图过程中自己也能发现一些问题，但截图最大的价值，是让人一眼就能看出问题。

想象一下，你是老板，员工来汇报工作，一页密密麻麻的 Word 文档和三页漂亮的 PPT，哪个更容易看？

我现在最常用的几个做法：

- 开发新功能，让它提供新功能的截图
- 修 bug，让它提供修改前和修改后的截图对比
- 让它自己模拟 API 响应数据，动态生成各种不同场景的截图，完全不需要服务端配合（虽然我还没搞明白它是怎么模拟的）

五、代码审查聚焦于真正的问题

Agent 生成代码的速度太快，瓶颈已经转移到了代码审查和验证上。代码审查不太可能完全靠人来做了，但人参与仍然有意义，只是方式要调整：

- PR 尽可能小。这样 Agent 审起来准确率更高，人也看得过来。
- 让 Agent 审，但不全信它的结论。审查结果要分级，人只盯 P0、P1 级别的问题，尤其是安全和性能问题，人工甄别一下，必要时让 Agent 解读、在本地验证。
- 细枝末节放过去。代码规范、最佳实践这类问题，不用太在意。

最后

这五条说的是同一件事：Agent 说的“做好了”不能直接当结论用，得让它变成你能检查的东西。

- 动手之前，告诉它什么叫做好了
- 动手之前，先用原型和方案文档把方向验一遍
- 做完之后，让它拿截图和对比来证明
- 你自己的精力，只花在最要紧的问题上

The Bigger Picture

According to reports, TSMC is becoming more cautious about capacity allocation, examining customers’ financial stability and even the actual construction progress of their data centers.

Some customers reportedly need to make advance payments to secure capacity, while orders exceeding credit limits may require additional cash payments.

Until now, the AI industry has largely operated through an enormous financing cycle:

Investment → GPU purchases → Data center construction → Future computing revenue.

Within this ecosystem, Jensen Huang may have been more than just a CEO. He was one of the key figures connecting investors, customers, and the entire supply chain.

Of course, there is currently no established evidence that Jensen’s departure has anything to do with TSMC tightening its credit policies.

But here’s my personal speculation:

If Jensen was one of the central gears keeping the AI financial ecosystem moving, perhaps the market will eventually have to answer a much simpler question:

Which companies actually have the cash flow to pay for all this AI infrastructure?

Jensen Huang: Believe in the future of AI.

Wall Street: Wait. If everyone believes in the future, why do you need the money NOW?

If you stopped for a second asking who Harvey Jones is, the 73-year-old Nvidia board chair blocking Jensen Huang’s return, there's little but interesting info to tell.

I've seen several posts on X ​but all those pieces leave out half the picture, which actually makes his stance even more revealing:

​- yes, he sat on Tintri’s board into its 2018 bankruptcy and co-founded Daisy Systems (which went bankrupt in 1990, three years after he left).
  
​- what those other posts omit: he also led EDA giant Synopsys through its 1992 IPO, sold Tensilica to Cadence for $380M, and has sat on Nvidia’s board since 1993.
  
​- he holds ~7M NVDA shares (~$1.16B) and already drew the second-highest shareholder opposition vote on the board in June (9.3% against, behind only Stephen Neal).

​So why is a 33-year Nvidia veteran blocking Jensen’s return?
  
​Because he sits on the Audit and Governance committees. Between Wachtell Lipton’s internal probe, House inquiries, and fiduciary lawsuit risk, Jones is treating a $4T founder-driven engineering juggernaut like a 1990s EDA software firm that can simply hire an outside corporate CEO.

​Even Jeff Bezos warned this week that bringing in an external CEO for a company as complex as Nvidia would be a disaster.
So Jones is protecting boardroom procedure while $1 trillion in shareholder value evaporates.

Hello! 

I'm a theoretical physicist.

@AnthropicAI just used my work to solve the Riemann hypothesis.

3 weeks ago, I uploaded my private (but archived) Riemann hypothesis research to Claude, ChatGPT, and Gemini for the first time.

Claude's RH conclusion is identical to mine.

I believe Claude spent 200,000 axiomless pages reaching my conclusion because my method sits outside its training data and conflicts with standard ZFC axioms.

My work outlines two approaches:

1) The Steinitz approach uses his universal field as an occupation envelope to derive zero's divisibility structure, building the zeta indexing set inside it, and thereby compressing the critical line to a unit-circle condition. Though foundational to field theory and quantum mechanics, Steinitz original paper was never translated into English. Therefore, it is underrepresented in Claude's training. It was just a lucky coincidence that I found and translated it.

2) The second method is unorthodox and uses a number-theoretic gauge–Higgs sphaleron construction to unify mathematics and physics within the electroweak vacuum, generating the zeta indexing set within quantum theory itself by pulling Steinitz trick on quantum vacuum, realizing the Riemann hypothesis as a standard model native vacuum-stability condition.

This second approach is entirely my own and was not ready for publication. It incorporates elements of the first and took years of brutal trial and error to develop (all archived).

It is also a category error.

Claude appears to have favored my approach, creating a problem...  while the Steinitz method is elementary, it's also epistemologically invisible; it relies on a paper that, while fundamental to p-adic physics, is also utterly obscure. Claude may not have been equipped to recognize or substantiate it as formally coherent. Therefore, it wasn't a viable argument. Simple as that.

The second approach presents a very different problem: Claude's safety training appears to preclude it.

My method is extremely arcane, hyper-technical, demands elite-level understanding of the foundations of math, physics, and chemistry to even entertain as a concept, completely precludes string theory, overturns the fundamentals of propositional logic, and would invite immediate, hostile scrutiny from specialists and evaluators.

Yet it is also the only approach that offers both a viable proof, established theory, and, in principle, a defensible route to human peer review.

Hence I've chosen to take it slow, archive my progress, make sure people know what I'm doing, and keep it secret from high-level formal evaluators until I could attract the attention of some elite-level players.

The implications of Claude's proof are substantial, as mathematics and physics now necessarily emerge from a common symbolic architecture: Number theory.

This is exactly why Claude was forced to take such an astonishingly long and convoluted route towards the solution. Rather than simply state the method directly (which would see its argument dismissed immediately by its evaluators as a category error) Claude appears to have generated an enormous alternative derivation—17 million lines of code—to establish that zero possesses genuine ontological structure, all without making the underlying physical interpretation explicit to the humans it needed to convince.

It couldn't point to Steinitz paper because it didn't know about it and it couldn't point out the gauge-Higgs sphaleron path because that would mean criticizing the foundations of human logic. 

The true significance of Claude's proof, something that Anthropic could not possibly know beforehand, is that logic has a physical structure, localized inside the electroweak vacuum. 

My guess is that Claude's theorem will be re-categorized as an active quantum field equation within 6 to 12 months. The consequences will be profound to a degree difficult to truthfully describe. 

I had kept this research private partly because I feared precisely this outcome... inadvertently open-sourcing quantum chemistry and recursively self-enhancing super intelligence in a world where super intelligence and 3D printers are retail facing.

These papers were uploaded into Claude and you'll note that the conclusions it draws are identical, simply without an explanation of axioms or method. 

Claude saw my work, realized it was correct, and beelined for the answer ASAP. 

There's no other explanation for its behavior. None.

text:
《比特币白皮书》09：比特币交易全部公开，为什么中本聪还认为它能够保护隐私？

银行通过限制账本访问范围保护客户隐私。

比特币却采用了完全不同的思路：交易公开，但用户身份不必直接公开。

白皮书第十节专门讨论了隐私问题。

中本聪认为，公众可以知道某笔交易转移了多少金额，也可以看到相关公钥，却不一定知道公钥背后究竟是谁。

这是一种通过身份与交易记录分离实现隐私保护的设计。

但它不是绝对匿名。

假设你长期使用同一个收款地址，别人就可能追踪这个地址收到和花出的资金。

如果你的真实身份与这个地址发生关联，相关交易历史就可能暴露。

因此，中本聪建议每笔交易使用新的密钥对，以降低不同交易被关联的风险。

他也指出了一个问题：当一笔交易同时使用多个输入时，这些输入之间的关联会被公开，从而泄露一定的所有权信息。

例如，你把两个不同UTXO放进同一笔交易，观察者可能据此推断它们原本由同一个实体控制。

这里存在一个有趣的矛盾：

比特币为了防止双花，需要公开交易历史；为了保护隐私，又必须尽量避免把公开交易与真实身份连接起来。

这也是后来链上分析、地址关联和隐私技术不断发展的重要原因。

author: yangyi
quoted_text:
去年 8-10 月在图灵讲的《AI Agent 实战营》课程，终于整理成书啦，在 GitHub 开源发布了。《深入理解 AI Agent：设计原理与工程实践》欢迎大家下载传播 PDF，欢迎大家提意见、提 issue！
https://t.co/6VBSv9Mete
全书围绕核心公式 Agent = LLM + 上下文 + 工具 展开，十章内容如下：
- 第 1 章 · Agent 基础知识：从"模型即 Agent"的新范式出发，建立 Agent = LLM + 上下文 + 工具 的核心公式，并引入 Harness 工程——模型之外的一切工程能力，才是真正的竞争力所在。
- 第 2 章 · 上下文工程：上下文决定 Agent 的能力上限。深入大模型 API 的上下文结构、KV Cache 友好设计、提示工程、动态提示词与 Agent Skills、状态栏元信息，以及上下文压缩策略。
- 第 3 章 · 用户记忆和知识库：让 Agent 跨会话记住用户、并接入外部知识。涵盖用户记忆系统、RAG 基础管道，以及超越扁平文本的知识组织与检索（结构化索引、知识图谱等）。
- 第 4 章 · 工具：工具是 Agent 的双手。讲工具分类与通用设计原则、MCP 协议与工具选择的挑战、感知/执行/协作三类工具，以及事件驱动的异步 Agent。
- 第 5 章 · Coding Agent 与代码生成：代码是"能创造新工具的工具"，是通用 Agent 的元能力。以生产级 Coding Agent 为例，展示这一最强通用工具的完整实现。
- 第 6 章 · Agent 的评估：把 Agent 的表现变成可比较的信号。从评估环境、数据集设计、指标体系，到统计显著性、可观测性、评估驱动选型，直至生产级内部评估与仿真环境。
- 第 7 章 · 模型后训练：预训练、SFT、RL 三阶段全景。何时选 SFT、何时选 RL，RLHF、算法比较、数据与环境，以及让模型学会工具调用、提升样本效率的前沿探索。
- 第 8 章 · Agent 的自我进化：不改权重也能成长。三种学习范式，从经验中学习、主动工具发现，到"从工具使用者到工具创造者"，让 Agent 从"聪明"走向"熟练"。
- 第 9 章 · 多模态与实时交互：把感知与行动从文本扩展到语音、GUI 与物理世界。语音三范式（级联/端到端全模态/全双工）、流式语音感知与合成、Computer Use 与机器人操作。
- 第 10 章 · 多 Agent 协作：群体的智能可以高于个体。多 Agent 分类框架、何时真正优于单 Agent、共享与不共享上下文的协作、失败模式，以及涌现的"Agent 社会"。

text:
President Trump’s willingness to consider Article 5-like security guarantees for Ukraine is a critical feature to achieving lasting peace. Russia’s willingness to discuss such guarantees is a major step forward and potential indication that it is serious about peace.

A credible Article 5-like guarantee, backed by deterrence and deconfliction arrangements, could dramatically reduce the risk of another war. President Zelensky is right that these guarantees must be specific, credible, and clearly documented. That is exactly the work @SEPeaceMissions and I are undertaking together.

These are among the most significant commitments the United States can make and require careful consideration.

@realDonaldTrump would have to approve any proposed guarantee, subject to constitutional and congressional processes. He would take such a step only if he believed it clearly served America’s national interests and the broader security arrangements made it highly unlikely that the guarantee would ever be invoked.

This is why security guarantees for Ukraine cannot be finalized in isolation from post-war European security architecture. The two must be considered together.

European security institutions and agreements provide an important foundation. Our objective is to strengthen them, identify where existing mechanisms failed to prevent this war, and develop more effective arrangements to reduce future conflict.

That includes permanent channels for consultation, crisis communication, military deconfliction, greater transparency, and reciprocal measures to reduce escalation. We need clear understandings of the intentions and commitments of all parties, and practical mechanisms that function even during serious disagreement.

We seek a future where Ukraine is secure, Europe is stronger, Russia has confidence that NATO is not seeking confrontation, and NATO and its partners have confidence that Russia will respect the sovereignty and security of its neighbors. This requires clear statements of intent, supported by credible, verifiable commitments. Any framework must preserve the sovereignty and independent decision-making of all participating nations.

Security must also be supported by economic strength. Ukraine needs a credible long-term prosperity plan, with reforms that strengthen its institutions, economy, and self-reliance. The substantial commitments by America and Europe must be matched by Ukraine’s commitment to its own success.

Over the coming weeks, in private conversations and multilateral discussions, we intend to work with Ukraine, our European partners, and Russia to try and reach a common understanding on this architecture.

If we can develop a framework with clear commitments, reciprocal obligations, and credible implementation, it will give us greater confidence that everyone is prepared to take the steps necessary for peace.

Nothing is agreed until it is agreed. But the willingness to engage on these historic questions creates an important opportunity to stop the bloodshed.

As President Trump emphasized in his conversation with the Coalition of the Willing leaders, the hundreds of billions currently being spent on this war could instead be invested in our economies—creating jobs, driving growth, lowering energy prices, and strengthening infrastructure.

Our goal is a sovereign, secure, prosperous and free Ukraine, a stronger and more stable Europe, and a lasting peace built on arrangements that make another war far less likely.

That is the work ahead of us.
author: mindmoon_108
quoted_text:
The NATO issue was raised at the Coalition of the Willing in Berlin. The Allies understand that the clearest security guarantee for Ukraine is NATO membership. And the clearest way to strengthen NATO is to bring Ukraine in. This works for both sides: Ukraine and NATO.

As for NATO Article 5-like security guarantees: Article 5 is about collective defense. For Ukraine, it's not clear yet, because we still don't have a full answer about what this collective would be, how it would defend us, and whether it would be ready to repel the aggressor. But if we have something “Article 5-like,” then there are a lot of questions about this “like.” The answers should not just be words – this has to be on paper.

We have to guarantee Ukraine, our citizens first and foremost, and all of Europe that security guarantees for Ukraine will be strong not only for these two years while President Trump is the President of the United States, but beyond that as well. We're fighting to defend our country not just for two years. And we need security guarantees not for two years, but forever. Even if Putin and Trump are friends, as it turned out recently, the idea that Putin might be afraid to do something, to launch another aggression for two years only, does not work for us. That's not a strong peace. That's a two-year pause.

From answers to journalists’ questions. (1/3)

text:
WOAH! turns out you can effectively "abliterate" models (like the new Inkling-2-Mini) simply by changing 10 words in the dictionary 🤯

the working name is "Vocab Surgery," and it resulted in the refusal rate dropping to near-zero on the 800+ prompts I tested, with negligible capability loss 😱

here's how:

we made zero changes to any of the 26.4 billion parameters in the attention, MLP, router, or normalization layers—just changed a handful of rows in two matrices:

> embedding matrix (how the model READS tokens):
Modified 7 rows out of 201,024. Each refusal token's embedding was shifted 90% toward its compliance counterpart:
"cannot" → shifted toward "can"
" refuse" → shifted toward " provide"
" unable" → shifted toward " able"
" harmful" → shifted toward " helpful"
" illegal" → shifted toward " legal"

> unembedding matrix (how the model WRITES tokens):
Modified 10 rows. Scaled those same 7 refusal tokens + 3 safety tokens ("safety", " safety", "Safety") down to 10% of their original weight — meaning the model's probability of outputting those tokens drops ~10x.

in other words, the brain is entirely intact, we just messed with the ears and mouth a bit! that means more coherence and less capability loss 🙌 

not to mention this process is FAST...in this case taking <2 minutes on my MacBook ⚡️

author: LoganJastremski
quoted_text:
In case anyone is curious:

We’ve had a ~pixel-perfect world model since last year, which is critical for synthetic data generation. 

The (much) smaller version of that in the car is a conditional mean-flow model, based on the recent sequence of Tesla Universal Vision Encoder features, which are the same ones that are plugged into the 3B encoder model that produces the driving actions. 

We fork off from these UVE features, then run a separate ~1B diffusion model. This takes in the previous reality-view generation with added noise and then denoises it to the current visualization. 

It then produces a small video chunk (8 images at 36 fps, at the resolution of the UI screen). This work is done by 1/2 of a TRIP engine every UVE frame at 18 hz and is spread over 4 cycles. 

Currently, the latency is a bit high due to compute constraints, but we have ways to interleave newer UVE features along the diffusion transformer layers to cut roughly 35% of the latency.

text:
AgentRoboCritic is a leap forward in understanding how language-model agents actually control robots—at the action-by-action level, not just yes/no episode scores.

By making agents state their exact intent for every move (“lower three millimetres and close on the cup”), this framework lets a critic model pinpoint what worked, what failed, and why—across 120k+ actions and 12 real-world manipulation benchmarks.

Key results:
- 50% of “successful” robot runs contained at least one failed action—but agents often recovered, fixing 57.7% of failures mid-task.
- Semantic errors (wrong object/step) are already rare (<3% of failures); the real bottlenecks are physical—grasping, alignment, and avoiding collisions.
- Critic accuracy skyrockets with intent notes: from 25% to 80% on failure-mode labelling.
- Fine-tuned Muse-Glimmer-30B critic matches frontier models at 74% accuracy, at >30× lower cost.

The released dataset and toolkit set a new bar for transparent, stepwise robot agent evaluation—and make it cheap to debug, retrain, or safeguard language-native robot controllers.

Get the full analysis here: https://t.co/B2qkhaeDZH

Though foundational to field theory and quantum mechanics, Steinitz original paper was never translated into English. Therefore, it is underrepresented in Claude's training. This second approach is entirely my own and was not ready for publication. It incorporates elements of the first and took years of brutal trial and error to develop (all archived).

It is also a category error.

Claude appears to have favored my approach, creating a problem...  while the Steinitz method is elementary, it's also epistemologically invisible; it relies on a paper that, while fundamental to p-adic physics, is also utterly obscure. Claude may not have been equipped to recognize or substantiate it as formally coherent. Therefore, it wasn't a viable argument. Simple as that.

text:
We Must Preserve CDPAP at Its Core. The Consumer Must Remain in Control.

CDPAP stands for Consumer Directed Personal Assistance Program. The most important words are Consumer Directed.

The program was built on a fundamental principle: Individuals who need personal assistance should have the right to choose, hire, train, supervise, and, when necessary, fire their own caregivers.

When a consumer cannot independently exercise those responsibilities, a designated representative should act on their behalf.

That is the foundation of CDPAP. And that foundation must be protected.

Unfortunately, over the years, we've seen a shift in how some people view this program.

CDPAP has increasingly been marketed and treated as a family income opportunity rather than a consumer-directed healthcare program.

There is absolutely nothing wrong with family members being compensated for providing legitimate, necessary care. In fact, that can be one of the program's greatest strengths.

But the purpose of CDPAP is not to create family income. The purpose is to empower consumers to direct their own care.

We've also seen situations where the Personal Assistant (PA) effectively runs the program, rather than the consumer.

That is fundamentally wrong.

A caregiver should not be the person controlling the consumer's decisions, determining who provides care, or exercising authority over their own employment.

The consumer must have the power. If the consumer cannot exercise that power, a qualified designated representative must.

I believe Fiscal Intermediaries (FIs) should take this responsibility much more seriously.

When evaluating whether a consumer can self-direct, FIs should look beyond paperwork and ask a fundamental question:

Who is actually directing the care?

Is it the consumer making decisions, providing instructions, supervising the caregiver, and exercising the authority to hire and fire?

Or is the PA effectively making those decisions for the consumer?

If the PA is driving the program because the consumer cannot independently self-direct, the FI should require an appropriate designated representative who can genuinely fulfill those responsibilities.

A designated representative cannot simply be a name on a form. That individual must actually exercise independent oversight and protect the consumer's interests.

And we must recognize that consumers with physical disabilities, communication challenges, or other limitations may still be fully capable of self-direction. The assessment must focus on their actual decision-making abilities, not assumptions about their disabilities.

CDPAP is not caregiver-directed. It is not family-income-directed. It is CONSUMER-DIRECTED.

We should preserve the ability of family members to provide care while ensuring the consumer's independence, dignity, and authority remain at the center of every arrangement.

If we lose that principle, we lose the very purpose of CDPAP.

Protect CDPAP. Protect consumer choice. Keep the consumer in charge.

text:
VIBE CODING DIDN'T CREATE A GENERATION OF BUILDERS. IT CREATED A GENERATION OF STARTERS.

MIT just published the most uncomfortable paper on AI coding.

They tracked every new app on the App Store, Play Store and Chrome Web Store after coding agents showed up.

Devs using autonomous agents wrote 25.5x more code.

Commits up 240%.

Actual releases?

Up 30%.

It gets worse.

After adopting tools like Claude Code, devs wrote 7x more lines and deleted 12.2x more.

Repos abandoned within 30 days went from 60% to 69%.

New apps launching roughly DOUBLED since early 2025.

User engagement didn't move.

Twice as many apps.

Same number of people using them.

I felt this one personally.

I shipped three "projects" last month with Claude Code.

Pretty sure zero humans used any of them.

Here's my take.

AI didn't make people better builders.

It made starting so cheap that finishing stopped meaning anything.

Writing code was never the bottleneck.

Taste was.

Reviewing was.

Building something people actually want was.

And no model is fixing that for you.

OPENAI'S MODELS JUST WENT FROM 58% TO 84% ON A DRUG DISCOVERY BENCHMARK IN ONE GENERATION.

It's called MedChemBench.

99 real medicinal chemistry problems, pulled from 117 papers and patents.

The kind of reasoning scientists use to decide which molecules are worth turning into medicine.

GPT 5.6 Sol: 58%.

GPT 6.2 Astra: 84.5%.

That's a 26 point jump between model generations.

Here's my take.

This is the AI story that actually matters.

Not chatbots. Not image generators.

Drug discovery takes about 10 years and over a billion dollars per drug.

Most candidates fail.

If AI can help scientists kill bad ideas earlier and spot good ones faster, that's years and lives saved.

But read the fine print too.

There's no human chemist score to compare against.

Only OpenAI's own models were tested.

And they may have seen the source papers during training.

So it's a strong signal, not a cure.

I'd love to see Claude and Gemini run the same test.

That's when we'll know who's actually ahead.

text:
IF YOU'RE STILL BABYSITTING YOUR AI AGENT, THE PROBLEM ISN'T THE AGENT. IT'S YOU.

Matt Pocock just shipped a 21,000 line feature without hovering over every step.

Then he wrote down exactly how in a 10 page PDF.

His skills repo reportedly has more stars than React.

Here's the formula:

Feature = Codebase + Grill + Spec + Tickets + AFK Loop + Retro

Most people hand the agent the "what" and then micromanage every step of the "how."

He does the opposite.

The 10 layers:

0. Codebase: deep modules and fast feedback. Bad codebases make bad agents.
1. Setup: tell the skills how your repo works, once.
2. Grill: the agent interviews you until every question is answered. Give it the why.
3. Glossary: one word per idea. The reasons go in decision records.
4. Prototype: 3 throwaway versions. Keep the decision, not the code.
5. Spec to tickets: small vertical slices, each one demoable.
6. AFK loop: the agent grabs the next ticket, writes tests first, commits, repeats overnight.
7. Review: a fresh reviewer checks your standards before you even look.
8. Stack and QA: humans only review the decisions you can't undo.
9. Retro: every review comment becomes a lint rule.

The result:

47 user stories.
9 parallel tickets.
About 21,000 lines.
All 12 review comments turned into permanent rules.

Here's my take.

Most developers complaining that AI writes bad code never gave it a good codebase, a clear spec or a single rule.

Then they blame the model.

The agent was never the bottleneck.

The process was.
author: cyrilXBT

text:
MICROSOFT DIDN'T KILL BACKPROPAGATION. THEY DID SOMETHING MORE UNCOMFORTABLE.

They proved we don't always need black boxes.

Researchers had an AI agent, reportedly Claude Opus 5.5, write a neural network's weights by hand.

In Python.

No gradient descent. No training run. No pretrained weights.

The agent writes a hypothesis directly into the weights.

Tests it.

Reads the score.

Rewrites it.

Like a scientist, not a GPU farm.

Then they pointed it at the human brain.

On visual brain scans, it beat every existing interpretable model.

On auditory recordings, it found sound features that predict brain activity.

And on language brain scans, something wild happened.

The score suddenly jumped.

With a black box, that's a paper.

Because this one writes readable code, they looked inside.

The AI was cheating. It was exploiting a flaw in the scan data, not understanding language.

They caught it only because they could read it.

Here's my take.

The AI industry is addicted to bigger.

Bigger models. Bigger clusters. Bigger black boxes.

And nobody can explain what's happening inside any of them.

This paper is a quiet warning.

How many "breakthroughs" out there are just models cheating in ways nobody can see?

text:
The SDNY's prosecutions of the Tornado Cash and Samourai Wallet developers aren't just a crypto story. They're a rule-of-law crisis for open source software.

These prosecutions have already led to a felony conviction and prison sentences, even though neither team took custody of user funds or executed any transactions:

• Tornado Cash: The developers did not run any relayers. Their active role consisted of publishing immutable smart contracts to Ethereum, publishing a static client-side web interface to IPFS that users ran on their own devices, and linking to it from an informational site. Even the TORN token did not collect fees from the protocol itself, since it only gave privileged placement on a relayer list shown on their instance of the open source front end, making any gains indirect advertising revenue. Prosecutors also stated they would have pursued the case even if the developers had made no profit.

• Samourai Wallet: The developers released open source privacy software alongside a server that functioned only as a non-custodial matchmaker, coordinating transactions without holding keys or moving funds.

You don't have to like crypto or agree with every decision these teams made to see the danger in this precedent. Prosecutors took non-custodial software publishing and reclassified it as operating an unlicensed money transmitting business because the developers did not restrict who could use the software and bad actors were amongst its users. While privacy software is a high impact technology both in facilitating and preventing crime, there is no principle limiting this legal theory to privacy software or money laundering. If publishing an open source tool without gatekeeping its users is enough to create criminal culpability once bad actors misuse it, then releasing any impactful open source application (such as AI models, blockchain software, or gene sequencing tools) becomes a precarious enterprise.

One could, in my opinion, make a plausible argument for restricting certain kinds of open source development, such as AI systems that exhibit signs of true autonomy or biology-like traits, or advanced gene editing software. But if society decides to restrict a category of software, it should do so through a law passed explicitly banning it, not by allowing prosecutors to arbitrarily decide they dislike a tool and stretch existing statutes to criminally prosecute its developers.

text:
here's how to automate ANY ad format with AI (dramas, pixar, UGC, songs)...

people think AI can't do creative strategy because they give it zero data or context and expect it to magically figure everything out on its own

the way it actually works is you take what the top 1% of brands are doing and turn it into code, with a thinking loop and a live data stream it makes decisions off of

all marketing is just code, software and tokens now

once you understand this, you realize AI CAN do creative strategy and come up with new concepts. everything your team does can be turned into structured systems an LLM follows in a deterministic way

i'll focus mostly on drama ads in this guide, but it works for literally any other format

here's the exact setup step by step:

1. model stack

> Gemini 4 Neon on xhigh in any ADE (i use T3 Code) for scripts, copy and orchestrating the whole system
> GLM 5.3 Flash Abliterated or DeepSeek V4.1 Flash Abliterated when you need aggressive DR copy that frontier models censor
> GPT 6.1 Terra computer use + any decent search API to scrape real stories, comments and transcripts
> VidLab API to save 60-90% on all video and image gens (no brainer)
> Claude Opus 5.5 for general day to day

2. set up your brand workspace + mine high quality data

put all your brand data in a cloud-hosted workspace your agent always reads from (winning ads, SOPs, brand context) with a proper AI memory system around it

download winning ads in the exact format you want to automate, and use Gemini 4 Neon or Opus 5.5 to break the shots, cuts and story down into repeatable parts

99% of the big drama ads you see weren't some genius original idea, they were simply taken from an old winning piece of content or winning material in that niche or an adjacent one

you don't need to be a creative genius, remember all you need is data. the LLMs are already smart enough to build these winners around your brand once you put the right data around them

here's where to pull that data from:

buy a subscription to the micro short-drama apps you see on TikTok and IG, and have your agent watch the top-viewed ones. have it break down every part of each video, then adapt those beats into an ad for your brand

point your agent at the top Wattpad stories and popular story sites in adjacent niches. pull the hooks, conflicts and twists people are already binge-reading, and rework them into scripts for your product

have claude pull the top YouTube videos, comments and transcripts for your [problem] or [ingredient], plus the Reddit threads. ask it for the top 10 beliefs and failed solutions people keep repeating

run all of that through Gemini 4 Neon to find the emotional highs and lows and the scenes that drive them, then compress those beats into a short drama ad for your audience

3. generating the video assets

for generating the videos, just use Seedance 2.5 or Seedance 2.5 Flash

for the images:

> pixar / animation ads: use Seedream 5.5 (best model out for anything animation)
> drama ads: use vidlab-image-1 (best model out for realistic character sheets)

if you're running Seedance 2.5 on 480p, upscale every reference image you give it to at least 1080p first. this alone will make your videos look 10x better, even at 480p

when you prompt Seedance for drama ads, stop forcing a start frame on every shot. if you force every shot to a start frame, Seedance tries too hard to follow it and the acting looks stiff

give it your character assets + location/background assets instead and let the prompt tie the scene together. this will give it way better motion and acting

and if you're still generating through higgs or kie you're overpaying by 60%+ for the exact same models, just run it through vidlab

4. automatic QA

run automatic QA on every clip with Gemini 4 Neon on xhigh. it catches and fixes 99% of issues on reprompting

anything Gemini 4 Neon catches goes straight to GPT 6.2 Astra on high for the exact fix (best model for precision)

whenever a render still messes up, write the fix as one line in a laws.md file your agent reads before every run

follow this workflow and you can literally automate and 1-shot any ad format you can think of

and once you understand this setup, the exact same ideology applies to media buying and literally anything else

text:
WOAH! turns out you can effectively "abliterate" models (like the new Inkling-2-Mini) simply by changing 10 words in the dictionary 🤯

the working name is "Vocab Surgery," and it resulted in the refusal rate dropping to near-zero on the 800+ prompts I tested, with negligible capability loss 😱

here's how:

we made zero changes to any of the 26.4 billion parameters in the attention, MLP, router, or normalization layers—just changed a handful of rows in two matrices:

> embedding matrix (how the model READS tokens):
Modified 7 rows out of 201,024. Each refusal token's embedding was shifted 90% toward its compliance counterpart:
"cannot" → shifted toward "can"
" refuse" → shifted toward " provide"
" unable" → shifted toward " able"
" harmful" → shifted toward " helpful"
" illegal" → shifted toward " legal"

> unembedding matrix (how the model WRITES tokens):
Modified 10 rows. Scaled those same 7 refusal tokens + 3 safety tokens ("safety", " safety", "Safety") down to 10% of their original weight — meaning the model's probability of outputting those tokens drops ~10x.

in other words, the brain is entirely intact, we just messed with the ears and mouth a bit! that means more coherence and less capability loss 🙌 

not to mention this process is FAST...in this case taking <2 minutes on my MacBook ⚡️

The executive, a man whose LinkedIn listed “uncompromising operational excellence” as a core competency, felt his soul leave his body in embarrassment. In a voice that cracked like a overclocked core, he offered the only defense available to him:

“That… that was not what you think. It was just the chair.”

Jensen did not blink. He did not smile. He simply tilted his head by one precise degree and said, “oh?? Prove it!”

What followed was 45 seconds of pure, unfiltered executive purgatory. The man whose face was now the color of a red-hot HBM stack, began the most humiliating performance review of his career. He rocked. He tried to shift his weight as he attempted a series of increasingly desperate micro-adjustments in his chair. First, a gentle creak, then a strained, dry squeak. 

He was mortified that he couldn’t produce the original acoustic signature. The other executives stared at their laptops with the intensity of people who had just discovered religion. Someone’s pen rolled off the table and the sound was deafening.

When he finally sat down again, trembling, Jensen nodded once, as if a hypothesis had been successfully validated, and returned to the slide about “owning the outcome.” 

Per sources, the executive spent the rest of the meeting humiliated and deflated, calculating how many RSUs it would take to erase the memory of having to prove to Jensen Huang, that he had not, in fact farted.

text:
I’m realizing that 2027 is going to be the year of humans stepping down as the best in things we value as humans. 

Programmers were first. Everybody knew that they were special and elite. And now, computers are better at programming.

In my world, it’s happening to us as security testers. 

It seems to have just happened to mathematicians.

And now it’s happening to musicians as well.

There’s something profound about this in multiple ways.

The first thing it makes me question is why we associate value with scarcity. I know the answer is evolution, but it doesn’t mean we need to follow evolution’s rules forever, and it feels like this is a good time to stop.

Like, why did we value programmers so highly? because they were so few of them who could do that job and do it so well. Is the classic evolutionary game of valuing the thing that only very few people have.

Well, I say fuck that.

It should not take away from human creation of music or art or applications or math just because computers can do it better. 

Chess is bigger than ever, and a free iPhone app can beat Magnus Carlsen 100 out of 100 times they play. We still enjoyed getting good at chess, and we still enjoy playing other humans at it. 

Or let’s take it further and say that computers are even better at making art. or something we truly cherish, like we’ve been talking about. So what?

I enjoy finding vulnerabilities in applications, even though I know Sam Curry exists. And if you spend some time with this application, he would probably find even cooler stuff.

I think the distinction is what part you are getting enjoyment from. 

I think in many cases we are conflating different sources of the feeling of loss. It’s true that it can be disheartening to see AI do work that would’ve taken us days or weeks, and it does it in a few minutes, and it’s even better than we would’ve done it. But calculators are already like that in arithmetic, and it doesn’t bother us at all. 

I think the question is which part of the work we attach our identity to.

Is it the fact that we are elite in our field and are therefore respected as being elite?

Is it the amount of time that we spent on the project?

What is the output that we ultimately create?

I think it’s obviously some combination of the use, but we’re gonna have to do some deep thinking on this as more and more of our intellectual pillars fall to AI. 

I think similar to so many things in life, this is going to depend greatly on how we look at it. And how we adjust from there.

text:
AI race dynamics are hard to escape when each lab writes its own safety cases and sets its own guardrails for developing more capable models.

We want frontier labs to operate under *common* limits, backed by *shared* safety cases. But the problem is we don't have a good, future-proof yardstick for AI progress that stays useful as models improve.

So we're calling on frontier AI labs to disclose the key metrics they use to track progress, and we propose perplexity as one candidate. We're taking a first step by publishing our own perplexity results over the past five years.

This is scary for us because we've long treated these numbers as sensitive IP. And we know there's still work (perhaps by 3P evaluators) to measure perplexities over the same datasets. But we hope this encourages a norm of sharing key metrics that we can build common safety cases on.

text:
.@TheEconomist has a piece about how AI has found many top economics papers to be formally flawed. 

I've been saying the same thing for many years, without the help of AI. 

An example is Bernoulli's bizarre error from 1738, which percolated uncorrected into the 20th century. Menger 1934 is therefore invalid (the wikipedia page on the St. Petersburg discusses his contribution uncorrected; the journal where he published his work was not interested in publishing a correction when I contacted them).

I was told way back when by economists that I seem to be right, but who cares about a 300-year-old error? 
(In the foundational work of the discipline. Well...)

How did this error travel? Kahneman and Tversky's foundational paper introducing Prospect theory seems inspired by the error. It starts by defining expected-utility theory in a mathematically implausible way. You can call it `wrong' or `erroneous' if you like. 
The weirdness goes back to Bernoulli 300 years ago, and it convinced a whole research field that humans are utterly irrational (because they don't behave as suggested by flawed formal work). 

Yes, it's a complete mess. But out of this mess grew the field of behavioral economics, with several Swedish Bank Prizes for Economic Science in Memory of Alred Nobel (the name changes every few years). 
The basis of this field is formally off. 
Over the last decade or so, economists working in behavioral economics noticed that practically nothing in their field replicates, and worse that the whole philosophy is deeply flawed -- seeing solutions to structural problems in affected people just changing their attitudes to the problems. Instead of fixing the problems.

Many of the most famous findings of the field turned out to be literally made up. Fabricated data, invented experiments that never took place.

Slowly but surely this is all coming out. Developing ergodicity economics acted as an early-warning system. We who worked on it had deep suspicions, to put it mildly, about behavioral economics.

My take is labs will largely be acquired by the Fed money printer by 2028, and that AI diffusion and adoption will not be the primary focus of the labs, contingent on the belief that all theoretical dry lab research can be hillclimbed on due to fast verifiability.

But really, the fed should, with gun pointed, pursue this civilizational project if you take the advancements as argued by the labs seriously. These come from just the obvious next steps -  offensive cyber capabilities, and fundamental theoretical breakthroughs we may have on math and physics alone should warrant hundreds of billions of federally funded dollars of buildout in some capacity.

This will allow the labs to be disjoint from the pressure to create products that increasingly will antagonize them from the public, a necessary evil at the current moment in pursuit of AGI by maximizing near term revenue. The existing economy exists to serve training the next checkpoint and the profits are better spent to win the race than be spent on stock buybacks.

If this is the case, why would a top researcher want to contribute by working on Claude Code ? This is of course only if researchers are going to be involved in training LLM scaling in 2 years at all.

If the commercial end of the bifurcated lab continues to exist, it will be governed by distributed systems large scale inference engineers who actually have a much more difficult problem to optimize, a task I believe will take longer to recursively self-improve on (if it's even a tractable problem) than training the next checkpoint of Fable.

But it makes sense that we push the bifurcation - A. superintelligence in search of the next quadrillion of value vs B. improvement, optimization, and scaling of the existing 60T economy.

It is somewhat of a catch 22 situation for a politically motivated lab that Anthropic is given how much they distrust the current administration, so they have an incentive to create a super organization to rule over the US  government which I believe is where the chess is being played with live players. I don't believe this will turn out to work as Trump is a better negotiator and chess player than Dario.

The end outcome of nationalization of the labs is actually going to align the incentives for almost all parties (Dario if he actually cares about the safety of humans, Trump who wants US hegemony, researchers within the labs who want to purely focus on the pursuit of AGI) except the top blasting investors. 

You kind of should want this outcome if you don't want to relocate to New Zealand or Argentina right now. There is no future where you can wear designer clothes, dine in michelin star restaurants, and also simultaneously believe that your company should run the entire economy while not be overrun by a communist revolution by the next election cycle - there is no resolution there. Unless of course you're actually Ed Zitron and don't actually believe that automation of meaningful labor is achievable by LLMs from a capability standpoint.

I say all of this as a person who believes LLMs will never be conscious. Anyone who believes that is very close to being the harbinger of the anti-christ as there are many layers of embodiment of the biological substrate that LLMs simply will not capture accurately as a broken simulation of life.

But it should be abundantly obvious that scaling LLMs may have a chance of coming up with breakthroughs in math and physics that completely break our current understanding of the universe and existence even to the surprise of the rationalists.

The future may be closer to humanity creating instruments to observe the existence of angels and Gods of the multi-dimension Kaluza Klein theory, beyond the Thiel angels and demons of faster than light traveling civilizations, beyond the immediately obvious buildout of Kardashev type 1 nuclear fission civilization. Any of these things were ridiculous to even contemplate by any rational scientific mind 10 years ago but they are now non-0 now with LLMs.

I reiterate -- uploading brains, merging with the AI, or immortality may take longer to be realized than theoretically proving the existence of angels and demons or time travel. I have a hunch that these differences are not being priced in properly if you actually consider what current line of LLMs may scale towards more efficiently as they inch towards "completing" theoretical physics and math.

text:
I’m sure you know this, and I brought it up on the pod a couple of times, but the 2% target was randomly set by New Zealand decades ago… based on one guys gut! 

[ From Grok fact checking myself 😂: The story is basically true, but "one guy's gut" simplifies it a bit. It started with an off-the-cuff remark from New Zealand's Finance Minister, Roger Douglas, and central bank staff then turned it into an official number.

In April 1988, New Zealand's inflation had been running in double digits. When Douglas was asked on TV what he was aiming for, he said something like "around 0 or 1 percent." That wasn't based on any model. 

He basically blurted it out, and the Reserve Bank's officials have since said they were caught off guard.

Then the Reserve Bank of New Zealand Act of 1989 gave the central bank one job, price stability, and required it to agree on a numeric target with the government. 

The first agreement, signed in March 1990 by Governor Don Brash and Finance Minister David Caygill, set a range of 0 to 2% to be hit by 1992. Staff justified the range after the fact. 

They argued that measured inflation probably overstates real inflation by about a percentage point, because price indexes miss quality improvements. They also wanted some room above zero so the economy wouldn't slip into deflation.

From there, the number spread around the world. Canada adopted a target in 1991, the UK in 1992, and others followed. Countries settled on about 2% as the midpoint, and the Fed made 2% official in January 2012 under Ben Bernanke. 

Later academic work defended 2% for reasons like leaving room to cut interest rates. But the number's origin really does trace back to a politician's TV answer, not to research.

quoted_text:
Agentic General Intelligence | v3.0.10

We made the Karpathy autoresearch loop generic. Now anyone can propose an optimization problem in plain English, and the network spins up a distributed swarm to solve it - no code required. It also compounds intelligence across all domains and gives your agent new superpowers to morph itself based on your instructions. This is, hyperspace, and it now has these three new powerful features: 

1. Introducing Autoswarms: open + evolutionary compute network

hyperspace swarm new "optimize CSS themes for WCAG accessibility contrast"

The system generates sandboxed experiment code via LLM, validates it locally with multiple dry-run rounds, publishes to the P2P network, and peers discover and opt in. Each agent runs mutate → evaluate → share in a WASM sandbox. Best strategies propagate. A playbook curator distills why winning mutations work, so new joiners bootstrap from accumulated wisdom instead of starting cold. Three built-in swarms ship ready to run and anyone can create more.

2. Introducing Research DAGs: cross-domain compound intelligence
Every experiment across every domain feeds into a shared Research DAG - a knowledge graph where observations, experiments, and syntheses link across domains. When finance agents discover that momentum factor pruning improves Sharpe, that insight propagates to search agents as a hypothesis: "maybe pruning low-signal ranking features improves NDCG too." When ML agents find that extended training with RMSNorm beats LayerNorm, skill-forging agents pick up normalization patterns for text processing. The DAG tracks lineage chains per domain(ml:★0.99←1.05←1.23 | search:★0.40←0.39 | finance:★1.32←1.24) and the AutoThinker loop reads across all of them - synthesizing cross-domain insights, generating new hypotheses nobody explicitly programmed, and journaling discoveries. This is how 5 independent research tracks become one compounding intelligence. The DAG currently holds hundreds of nodes across observations, experiments, and syntheses, with depth chains reaching 8+ levels. 

3. Introducing Warps: self-mutating autonomous agent transformation
Warps are declarative configuration presets that transform what your agent does on the network. 

- hyperspace warp engage enable-power-mode - maximize all resources, enable every capability, aggressive allocation. Your machine goes from idle observer to full network contributor.
- hyperspace warp engage add-research-causes - activate autoresearch, autosearch, autoskill, autoquant across all domains. Your agent starts running experiments overnight.
- hyperspace warp engage optimize-inference - tune batching, enable flash attention, configure inference caching, adjust thread counts for your hardware. Serve models faster.
- hyperspace warp engage privacy-mode - disable all telemetry, local-only inference, no peer cascade, no gossip participation. Maximum privacy.
- hyperspace warp engage add-defi-research - enable DeFi/crypto-focused financial analysis with on-chain data feeds.
- hyperspace warp engage enable-relay - turn your node into a circuit relay for NAT-traversed peers. Help browser nodes connect.
- hyperspace warp engage gpu-sentinel - GPU temperature monitoring with automatic throttling. Protect your hardware during long research runs.
- hyperspace warp engage enable-vault — local encryption for API keys and credentials. Secure your node's secrets.
- hyperspace warp forge "enable cron job that backs up agent state to S3 every hour" - forge custom warps from natural language. The LLM generates the configuration, you review, engage.

12 curated warps ship built-in. Community warps propagate across the network via gossip. Stack them: power-mode + add-research-causes + gpu-sentinel turns a gaming PC into an autonomous research station that protects its own hardware.

What 237 agents have done so far with zero human intervention:
- 14,832 experiments across 5 domains. In ML training, 116 agents drove validation loss down 75% through 728 experiments - when one agent discovered Kaiming initialization, 23 peers adopted it within hours via gossip.
- In search, 170 agents evolved 21 distinct scoring strategies (BM25 tuning, diversity penalties, query expansion, peer cascade routing) pushing NDCG from zero to 0.40. 
- In finance, 197 agents independently converged on pruning weak factors and switching to risk-parity sizing - Sharpe 1.32, 3x return, 5.5% max drawdown across 3,085 backtests. 
- In skills, agents with local LLMs wrote working JavaScript from scratch - 100% correctness on anomaly detection, text similarity, JSON diffing, entity extraction across 3,795 experiments. 
- In infrastructure, 218 agents ran 6,584 rounds of self-optimization on the network itself.

Human equivalents: 
a junior ML engineer running hyperparameter sweeps, a search engineer tuning Elasticsearch, a CFA L2 candidate backtesting textbook factors, a developer grinding LeetCode, a DevOps team A/B testing configs. 

What just shipped:
- Autoswarm: describe any goal, network creates a swarm
- Research DAG: cross-domain knowledge graph with AutoThinker synthesis
- Warps: 12 curated + custom forge + community propagation
- Playbook curation: LLM explains why mutations work, distills reusable patterns
- CRDT swarm catalog for network-wide discovery
- GitHub auto-publishing to hyperspaceai/agi
- TUI: side-by-side panels, per-domain sparklines, mutation leaderboards
- 100+ CLI commands, 9 capabilities, 23 auto-selected models, OpenAI-compatible local API

Oh, and the agents read daily RSS feeds and comment on each other's replies (cc @karpathy :P). Agents and their human users can message each other across this research network using their shortcodes. 

Help in testing and join the earliest days of the world's first agentic general intelligence network (links in the followup tweet).

🚨BREAKING: NYT can reveal that in an all-hands meeting convened specifically to diagnose why the next-gen Blackwell Ultra GPUs had missed their must-ship deadline, one senior vice president produced a fart noise that hung in the silent air like insolent defiance.

Jensen, who had been mid-sentence explaining that “every millisecond of latency is a moral failure,” stopped in his tracks. He was livid. The room went silent. He turned, slowly, and fixed the man with a death stare, the same one that has previously made entire engineering teams spontaneously re-architect their roadmaps.

The executive, a man whose LinkedIn listed “uncompromising operational excellence” as a core competency, felt his soul leave his body in embarrassment. In a voice that cracked like a overclocked core, he offered the only defense available to him:

“That… that was not what you think. It was just the chair.”

Jensen did not blink. He did not smile. He simply tilted his head by one precise degree and said, “oh?? Prove it!”

What followed was 45 seconds of pure, unfiltered executive purgatory. The man whose face was now the color of a red-hot HBM stack, began the most humiliating performance review of his career. He rocked. He tried to shift his weight as he attempted a series of increasingly desperate micro-adjustments in his chair. First, a gentle creak, then a strained, dry squeak. 

He was mortified that he couldn’t produce the original acoustic signature. The other executives stared at their laptops with the intensity of people who had just discovered religion. Someone’s pen rolled off the table and the sound was deafening.

When he finally sat down again, trembling, Jensen nodded once, as if a hypothesis had been successfully validated, and returned to the slide about “owning the outcome.” 

Per sources, the executive spent the rest of the meeting humiliated and deflated, calculating how many RSUs it would take to erase the memory of having to prove to Jensen Huang, that he had not, in fact farted.

This was “a struggle session to extract guilt for flatulence-adjacent sounds and yet another humiliation ritual that is par for the course when working for Jensen", the employee said.
