quoted_text:
The context here is that it was put to me that loads of people protesting outside parliament on the day of the vote of this English ethnicity Bill might influence sympathetic MPs on the right to vote against it because they believe they have a support base.

I think that is extremely unlikely. Simply because those MPs would be taking a huge risk to be seen to be representing 'ethnonationalists', but they will also (correctly) conclude that even if they did, those people would never vote for them or support them in any meaningful way anyway. 

Think of it like going on strike (I.e withholding labour) to get concessions. It only works if you are doing valuable labour in the first place. If you never turn up to work anyway, or the employer hates you, they don't care if you withhold your labour.

Nationalists attempting to 'influence' other political factions is a write off now, because those other factions know that any support they give will never be reciprocated.

It's either give up trying to influence others and just pursue agency for yourselves or bust. But you can't persuade people when you have no meaningful leverage, no trust, and no reason whatsoever for the people you are trying to persuade to care.

text:
The 2% inflation target was randomly set by a dude in New Zealand decades ago… based on his gut! 

Grok says: It started with an off-the-cuff remark from New Zealand's Finance Minister, Roger Douglas, and central bank staff then turned it into an official number.

In April 1988, New Zealand's inflation had been running in double digits. When Douglas was asked on TV what he was aiming for, he said something like "around 0 or 1 percent." That wasn't based on any model. 

He basically blurted it out, and the Reserve Bank's officials have since said they were caught off guard.

Then the Reserve Bank of New Zealand Act of 1989 gave the central bank one job, price stability, and required it to agree on a numeric target with the government. 

The first agreement, signed in March 1990 by Governor Don Brash and Finance Minister David Caygill, set a range of 0 to 2% to be hit by 1992. Staff justified the range after the fact. 

They argued that measured inflation probably overstates real inflation by about a percentage point, because price indexes miss quality improvements. They also wanted some room above zero so the economy wouldn't slip into deflation.

From there, the number spread around the world. Canada adopted a target in 1991, the UK in 1992, and others followed. Countries settled on about 2% as the midpoint, and the Fed made 2% official in January 2012 under Ben Bernanke. 

Later academic work defended 2% for reasons like leaving room to cut interest rates. But the number's origin really does trace back to a politician's TV answer, not to research.
author: Jason
quoted_text:
I think the Fed is about to make another mistake on December 9th. Financial conditions have tightened massively. For example, @SpaceX, an investment grade company, just raised secured debt financing at an 8.259% interest rate versus below 6% for its unsecured bond offering at the time of its IPO. 

The cost of equity capital has also increased materially with the recent substantial decline in the stock market. 

The Fed’s 2% inflation ambition is misguided. Geopolitical risk and the required investment in global military spending, de globalization and tariffs, and the massive AI infrastructure and related energy investment are features of the world that did not exist when the 2% target was set. 3% inflation is a more realistic ambition in the new world. 

The Fed will put the U.S. and world in recession if it continues to raise rates in a failed attempt to drive inflation to 2%. 

Tell me why I am wrong.

text:
The bears are having their moment.

After predicting a top in the AI trade every month for the last 4 years, the bears finally got their moment last week.

However, in 3 to 6 months, we are going to look back at this correction and realize it was just that: a correction.

There is a widespread narrative right now that Nvidia, $NVDA, is quite literally going to collapse. This is a stock that was trading at a record high on October 6th, worth nearly $6 trillion, and the inventor of the most advanced chips in the world (it's not even close).

That's how deeply pessimistic sentiment has become over the last seven weeks.

Even if Nvidia produced half as much revenue as they are guiding for their next fiscal year, this company would still produce close to $400 billion in annual revenue.

Meanwhile, the S&P 500 has posted three consecutive quarters with earnings growth above 25% and eight straight quarters of double-digit growth.

And, sentiment flipped so quickly that the S&P 500 closed the week 4.1 standard deviations below its 50-day moving average on Friday. Not even 2020 and 2008 saw such an occurrence.

The reality is that AI truly is the "next big thing" and the AI buildout is only accelerating.

Bears will sound smart, bulls will make money.

text:
I 100% agree with this, it is the single most important metric for TAO holders. It's available on https://t.co/nyjjBmIF3g thanks to the hard work of @bloomberg_seth. 

It comes with two big takeaways:
1. The trend of coverage is sharply higher, driven by increasing subnet team buys and reallocation of emissions towards those subnets via dTAO. TAO's fundamentals are moving in the right direction.

2. The level of coverage, Bittensor's "budget deficit", is still gaping. That means much more TAO is issued and saleable than is structurally demanded today, and is the reason for the large divergence between TAO's price and the network KPIs.

In my view, the deficit calls for responsible adjustments to policy to increase new TAO demand and reduce new supply, such as increasing protocol fees and diverting unproductive issuance to target a balance between TAO supply and demand. In this way we can balance the interests of Bittensor stakeholders with those of TAO holders.

Too heavy-handed of changes and we risk suffocating the growth. But if we ignore the deficit altogether, we risk not learning the lessons of past DePIN projects who also achieved incredible KPIs and growing revenues, but ultimately failed due to the inability to convince investors to finance their growth.

For Bittensor to avoid the same fate, TAO must become money.

Thesis: For the first time in human history, there will be no adapting. 

“We’ll have new jobs” - Not this time.

What we’re used to is new technology taking our old jobs, creating new ones, that we can adapt to. This technology, on the other hand, will take our old jobs, along with the new ones it’ll create.

Why? This technology is us, but better.

This extends on a piece I wrote in 2023, titled ‘The Population Curse’, which states how such a paradigm will yield second-order consequences that leave us stranded in our own economic environments, turning us into a burden, rather than a boon.

Akash Compute Forwards is a design for a market where you can book GPU power in advance, at a fixed price:

▫️ You reserve a full server (8 GPUs) for one month, in a given region
▫️ Prices come only from the market's own daily auction
▫️ Gains and losses are paid in dollars every day, so nobody can walk away from a loss
▫️ Anonymous users put down 100% of the value. Verified users put down less, with a backer and a safety fund behind them
▫️ You get real GPU time, and validators check every hour that the server is actually running

The simulation is already available to try.
To learn more about Akash, read our article: https://t.co/i9tLLco7ee

text:
Pinterest, Spotify and Etsy are increasingly emphasizing human “taste” as a competitive edge. Some recent examples: 

Spotify co-CEO Gustav Söderström in Q1 2026 earnings call: 

“Some of the things in the world are facts that can be easily commoditized by LLMs, [such as the capital of Texas]. Other things are not so easily commoditized. And it turns out luckily for us, taste is not easily commoditized because it's not a fact, it's an opinion.

It differs between people, it differs between regions, it differs between people in those regions and use cases. And on top of that, it changes weekly…So, for this reason, we do invest quite a lot in something like our large personalization model, basically our own taste model.”

Pinterest CEO Bill Ready in Q2 2026 earnings call: 

“Our scale and the unique human curation that occurs on our platform have fueled our proprietary Taste Graph, with more than 80 billion monthly searches on Pinterest. 

The vast majority of searches are visual, and over half are commercial. There are also more than 16 billion boards created on our platform. We have a uniquely valuable signal of human taste and curation at scale. 

This enables us to train our AI with a deep understanding of taste, context, and intent that gets more personalized every time a user comes back. This powerful feedback loop is what helps users discover what they want before they have the exact words, brand, or product in mind. That’s why so many commercial journeys begin on Pinterest.”

Etsy CEO Kruti Patel Goyal in Q3 2026 shareholder letter: 

“Etsy’s challenge has never been a lack of choice - it's helping each shopper find what's uniquely right for them. With rich and expanding data on both our buyers and our inventory, we’re well positioned to build on-site shopping assistants that understand buyers' tastes and intent more deeply and connect them with the right items in even more powerful ways than off-site agents.”

quoted_text:
The Quiet Machine That Started Writing the Network

Most people still treat Bittensor as a story about emissions. That frame is outdated.

Engy (SN53) is the clearest example of a subnet where external demand is now large and consistent enough that the team can recycle real revenue into permanent alpha burns while reinvesting the rest into the one thing that was bottlenecking them: high-end inference capacity.

Over the past 30 days Engy served more than 3.11 trillion tokens. Daily peaks on Kimi K3.1 Pro have repeatedly crossed 50 billion. Cache rates are extremely high (~90%), which compresses revenue per token, yet absolute dollars remain material. Days in the mid-to-high teens of thousands have become routine. One recent day cleared ~$23k after cache. These are customers paying for inference, not emissions.

A large share of that revenue has gone into alpha buybacks and burns. Cumulative since August is approaching half a million dollars, with the monthly pace accelerating. A single recent burn used 660+ TAO to remove ~17,500 alpha permanently. Supply removed, funded by external usage.

They have been capacity-constrained on top-end hardware. B300 systems have already been purchased and are waiting to be racked. Additional data-center capacity is expected in the new year. Pricing on some models was adjusted upward (while remaining far cheaper than official APIs) specifically to protect reliability while the fleet expands. This is a supply problem being solved with the cash the demand itself is generating.

Gamma changes the next phase. Engy was an early adopter. Because Gamma is a network-level credit, any other subnet that enables it can accept it. Subnets can also direct portions of their emissions toward buying Gamma from providers they actually use. When that scales, the largest reliable inference providers become infrastructure that other subnets can pay for with their own emissions.

There is also a quieter signal that is easy to underweight. Const has also been using Engy as the inference backend for coding agents committing directly to Bittensor’s own repositories. The person who built the system is now building on one of its subnets for production work.

Emissions still dominate the broader network. What has changed is that a few subnets now have a second engine. For Engy that engine is already large enough to fund both buybacks and the next tranche of capacity. The B300s sitting offline today are a response to demand that already exists.

Real external revenue. A high percentage returning to the token via burns. A clear path to expanding the physical capacity that generates it. That combination is still rare.

We are at a critical juncture in our civilization, approaching super-intelligence via RSI. One encouraging thing I am seeing in the discourse is a shift away from thinking purely in terms of safety and an increased focus on whether the future we are racing towards is conducive to human flourishing.

We should, of course, avoid X-risk. 
But there's more to life than just being alive. We want humans to not just exist, but also thrive! The dangers from ASI are not only purely X-risk related, but also pertaining to human disempowerment. Unfortunately, as I've written in a recent article on handoverism, even the positive visions of post-AGI look not so good for most humans.

Whether we are racing towards a good future, not merely *any* future, should enter the conversation more when discussing the pace of progress.

text:
AI逆向时代：闭源已成徒劳，开源才是出路

朋友们，时代变了。
过去我们以为，把代码编译成二进制、锁进黑盒，就能守住核心。现在，这个逻辑正在被AI彻底撕开。
Claude Code、Codex、Grok Build 这类AI Agent，已经能直接接入 Ghidra、IDA 等逆向工具，把二进制、固件、APK、Electron应用一层层拆开，还原出逻辑，再重写成可运行的代码。游戏反编译、驱动重写、协议破解、功能克隆……这些曾经需要专业团队几个月甚至几年的工作，现在一个人+一个AI Agent，几天甚至几小时就能推进一大步。
闭源不再等于安全，只是把“被逆向”的时间从“几乎不可能”变成了“迟早的事”。
那为什么还要死守闭源？
•AI能逆向，你却控制不了叙事。 别人逆向出来的版本，可能残缺、带偏见，甚至被恶意修改。你自己开源，反而能主导正确的实现与演进。
•安全靠审查，不靠隐藏。 闭源是黑盒，漏洞藏到出事才发现；开源是白盒，全球眼睛帮你找问题。AI时代，隐藏的成本远高于被看见的成本。
•生态比护城河更值钱。 社区贡献、二次创新、跨平台适配、长期维护……这些是闭源公司用人力和金钱硬堆也堆不齐的。你开放，反而能让项目活得更久、更强。
•信任正在重新定价。 用户、开发者、企业，越来越愿意选择能看懂、能修改、能自托管的东西。闭源正在变成一种“额外风险”，而不是优势。
所以，请开源。
不是因为“开源很崇高”，而是因为在AI逆向已经成为常态的今天，闭源的边际收益正在快速归零，甚至转负。
把你真正有价值的部分——架构思想、业务洞察、持续迭代能力——放到明处。让代码被看见、被改进、被信任。
闭源曾经是壁垒，现在更像是一座正在被AI拆除的围墙。 与其等别人拆完再重建，不如你自己开门，把路修好。
开源吧。 在这个AI可以逆向一切的时代，真正难被复制的，从来不是代码本身，而是你愿意把它交给社区共同进化的勇气和远见。

text:
Yes to all of this. As agents take on more and more long running project work, and you have swarms of agents that parallelize work against a goal, the agent harness and architecture for orchestration will have to evolve. 

One of the biggest shifts is how those agents collectively share their knowledge, keep track of the tasks, and also coordinate with human users. This in theory is technically straightforward, but there’s a ton of complexity to get right to ensure agents can both get access to the revenant resources without too much or little exposure.

There are a lot of lessons to pull from based on how people already do this kind of work together (people share their files, have computers to work with, community in chats and inboxes, and so on). But equally the primitives need to be able to enable this work at a throughput far higher than people, and in a world where agents can much more easily become a vector of security risk. 

Going to be super fun building out this next generation of how agents operate. Lots of opportunity here both for horizontal and vertical specific approaches to bring this to life.

author: betashop
quoted_text:
founders: if you haven't created a company.md yet, 
do it right now.

VCs are already running your deck through AI. they drop the PDF into Claude or ChatGPT and start asking questions before they ever talk to you.

the problem: decks are built for eyes, not agents. charts become pixels. the AI fills the gaps with guesses, and then it diligences the guesses.

so we built something for their agents instead.

our company.md is a ~1000 line plain text file (and growing by the day). it's the deck, plus everything a technical partner would spend three weeks of diligence digging for:

• the deck, slide by slide, in words
• our full tech stack, layer by layer. surfaces, connectors, agent harness, fleet orchestration, models, skills, MCP, strategy authoring, runtime, exit engine, simulation venue, data pipeline, signing, telemetry, billing, infra, security model
• for every layer: what it is, how it works, the main technologies, its scale, and what's proprietary vs open source
• every MCP tool and every agent skill, listed and linked to the public repos
• a repo map: what lives where, public and private
• anonymized profiles of our top customers. what they build, how they pay, how they use their own AIs to drive ours. including the ones who left, and why
• every number carries the date it was last checked

so a partner can ask their Claude "how does order signing work?" or "what's actually proprietary here?" or "which customers churned and why?" and get a real answer in our words, not a guess from a screenshot.

what we learned building it:

1. write it for AI readers, and say so in line one
2. date every number. models trust what they can place in time
3. mark proprietary vs open source on every layer. it's the first thing a technical investor asks
4. include the customers who churned. an agent trusts a doc that isn't all good news
5. one link that always serves the latest version, on every slide of the deck
6. keep it in sync with the deck. any mismatch is the first thing their agent will flag

it's become the most effective tool in our pitch arsenal.

Before: Investors skimmed the deck prior to the meeting:

Now: 
+ agent take the first meeting and prep their human investors

text:
In case anyone is curious:

We’ve had a ~pixel-perfect world model since last year, which is critical for synthetic data generation. 

The (much) smaller version of that in the car is a conditional mean-flow model, based on the recent sequence of Tesla Universal Vision Encoder features, which are the same ones that are plugged into the 3B encoder model that produces the driving actions. 

We fork off from these UVE features, then run a separate ~1B diffusion model. This takes in the previous reality-view generation with added noise and then denoises it to the current visualization. 

It then produces a small video chunk (8 images at 36 fps, at the resolution of the UI screen). This work is done by 1/2 of a TRIP engine every UVE frame at 18 hz and is spread over 4 cycles. 

Currently, the latency is a bit high due to compute constraints, but we have ways to interleave newer UVE features along the diffusion transformer layers to cut roughly 35% of the latency.

text:
can you hedge onchain costs the way airlines hedge fuel?

tested it on six years of data.

every crypto business pays costs it doesn't control: borrow rates, perp funding, gas.

the tools to hedge them today don't fit:
→ perps can liquidate you
→ options need a volatility market that doesn't exist for these rates
→ prediction markets pay $1 or $0, which you can't size to a bill

so i tested a simpler shape: a capped hedge.

1/ you pick a level
2/ if the 30-day average goes above it, you get paid the difference, up to a limit
3/ paid automatically in usdc
4/ every payout is fully funded onchain up front. no margin, no liquidation

what i found

for buyers: costs a little more in a normal month, cuts the bad ones.

ethereum gas:
> worst month: $3,845 → $2,195
> month-to-month swings: $820 → $180

for the pool: it paid.

usdc borrow rates, 2020–2026:
> $2.72m a year in premiums
> $0.24m in claims
> no losing year. even 2023, the worst, held

what's still broken
→ prices run 3–10x actual claims, because the model leans on the past year
→ funding rates keep moving once they start, which gives buyers an edge over the pool

those are the next problems i'm solving.

tradfi has had this for decades, behind paperwork and $1m minimums.

onchain it can start at $100.

author: Slayed_eth
quoted_text:
You need to hear my return from London story:

I was still not 100% adjusted so I wake up at 3ish am and start just texting my mother. Yes my mother. 

Around 4 am she tells me get some sleep. I said you're so right. I try to sleep. I can't.

It's 7am, I still can't sleep. I have my return flight at 3PM. I started to get paranoid.

I'm so tired if I sleep, I think I will sleep through my alarm and I'll be stuck in London forever. 

We need to pack NOW!! 

So I get up, and almost die.
Omg. I'm hungover. I can barley move. How are we gonna pack?

So I start picking up everything and just THROWING it into the bag.

It became a fking MOUNTAIN of clothes. 
I'm telling you it was a mountain. 

I have no idea how im gonna close this suitcase. 

So I lay on it and it's not even close to closing and I just say okay. This is not an option. I need to figure something out.

A brilliant thought hit me that would curse me later

Wear all your biggest, warmest stuff, and it will make space. 

Sure enough. It worked (after leaving some stuff behind on purpose as well, some of which I have still to discover because I was hungover full of anxiety thinking im gonna miss my flight in 8 hours, this is happening early in the morning remember?!).

Important pre story:
On the way here, I had to take out my laptop from my suitcase. I did not remember I put it in their but I was using a gift bag, those paper bags you get from buying nice things to hold it. I only bought a cologne, but it was a perfect bag on the way there.

In this scenario I had to open my suitcase in front of everyone but only just a bit, stick just enough that my hand can get through and pull out the laptop in front of everyone , and try to close it again. 

The issue became, now I had a fully exposed laptop. 

I bought a cologne and it coincedently came with a strong paper bag that could perfectly fit my laptop. To me, this is God at work, making everything easy for me. Life always works like this to me, thank you God.

I was asleep when I got on the flight to London, when I woke up on that flight, the bag looked like I got into a fight with it, torn and abused. 

This bag now, cannot be trusted. It's 75% ripped and my laptop will fall. It will not last the way back, I'm sure of it.

This makes me even more paranoid. My suitcase, the exposed laptop, I must get to this airport EARLY.

So I check in like 8 hours way too early. 

I find a place with laptop bags. their cheapest one was 185 british pounds, for the ugliest mfr ive ever seen. Whatever.

A hangover from hell, just wanting to be home, I rather die than carry anything. 

but I look around, and I'm so early my flight isn't even showing on the boards. This makes me freak out even more.

I thought flights always show up on the boards (I'm never this early)... Am I in the right place? 

How did everyone let me through just scanning tickets and telling me to go here? Who took my luggage! If it's not on the boards with every flight, where will it go? 

I assume my luggage is lost forever. 

I cannot do anything about that now. 

Grok started here. I said what is going to happen, did I just lose my luggage and I can't even find my flight on the board.

It assures me i'm fine and this is normal, I just showed up too early, and that luggage is done from some automatic conveyor belt thingies and it's coming. 

I don't believe it, but now I'm still not convinced grok is right about the boarding.

so every 10-30 minutes now, I can't even relax.

 Will my flight show up on the boards? Am I in the right area? and again, how did anyone let me into this place!!

I think about having a drink but no, I know at this point I'm so lost even a single drink will make sure I am stuck in London forever. 

Eventually, the flight shows up on the board. I am saved. 

Now remember, I'm in all my biggest warmest stuff. At this point I am not sweating at all. And I smell good. 

I board my flight and what seemed like a genius idea at the time (the giant jackets/sweater/sweatpants), becomes a very bad idea, very quickly:

- I start sweating within the first 10 minutes
- I start getting my stomach rumbling within the first 10 minutes but its nothing for now 

Eventually my stomach starts getting worse and worse. It's diarrhea.

My entire flight turned into me sweating for 10 hours straight due to what i'm wearing, and spending half the flight on the toilet which I had to get someone to move everytime I wanted to go. 

I'm sorry whoever that was. 
He's endured 10 hours of my sweat and bathroom breaks the flight as well. 

I'm still not home. Layover.

You see, when I was headed to London, I noticed this layover. I do not do layovers.

I had a plan, in London, fix/upgrade the seats, worst case I stay a day longer.

I forgot I had that plan and my flight just landed somewhere that isn't my home.

So I get off the plane, get my luggage, and do my first ever layover. Which includes exiting the airport.

I am on the streets now and have no idea where to go, and Grok comes in and starts location tracking me telling me if I'm walking in the right direction or not.

Grok literally saved my life. 

I was ready to give up and just call an uber to drive however long it would've taken, anything but another plane.

I end up getting my bags rechecked, finding the terminal, and we have a delay. Then another delay. 

Now also smelling like raw dumpster after sweating and sh*tting for 10 hours. 

The return flight eventually gets here, and it's pretty empty. I get a seat by myself by the grace of God.

I tell Grok to book me the nearest hotel, I need rest. 

I get to this hotel and maybe have 2 hours sleep because now I'm on different timezones, after time traveling and this is the time I'd normally be up. 

Get an Uber at like 6-7am and I'm finally on the ride home. My house is a little over 2 hours from the airport.

I didn't look at the type of car. 
The UBER shows up in a Tesla. 

I never considered this. His first words were "I'm surprised you accepted a Tesla" 

idkk why he would say this such thing, teslas are nice I like them.

Halfway home he says why, it needs to recharge. 

This recharge took us off the quick path home and adds another hour + 30mins. 

Everything on the way home was cursed. 

The trip was worth it and amazing 10/10.

Missing things I'm sure, but I made it.
Alive, but barely. 

Now it's 5am and my sleep schedule is still on Londons time zone but we'll deal with that later. 

attached is the bag before I got in a fight with it headed into London. And my mothers texts, and groks reply to yall.

Lets do it again.

text:
刷了一圈AI证明黎曼猜想的大新闻，我反手把李永乐老师2018年那期讲黎曼猜想的经典视频翻出来考古了。

哪怕过了8年，这期17分钟的视频依然是普通人看懂黎曼猜想最好的入门课。当年是因为数学界大佬阿蒂亚爵士宣布证明了猜想，李老师顺势开了个三期系列，第一期上来就抛了个极其反直觉的等式：1+2+3+4一直加下去，全体自然数的和竟然等于负十二分之一。

重温一遍还是觉得很震撼，几个核心点特别有意思：

别被直觉骗了。按常规加法，正数越加越大肯定是无穷大。但数学家通过解析延拓，把原本不收敛的级数延拓到了更广的复平面上，才得出了这个违背常识的数值。
这绝不是数学家的文字游戏。负十二分之一这个看起来很荒谬的结果，在现代物理学里是真能派上用场的，很多前沿理论的计算都绕不开它。
顶级难题也能听个明白。李老师最厉害的地方，就是能把悬赏一百万美元、困住人类一百五十多年的千禧年难题，拆解成用基础数学就能跟得上的逻辑。

每次数学界出大新闻，满屏都是各种看不懂的论文和术语，回头看这种把底层逻辑讲透的硬核科普，反而觉得特别过瘾。

text:
It is both intriguing and deeply unsettling that AI is approaching a point where it will understand what it can do—what it must do—in orders of magnitude, beyond our ability to "Undo" what it may do.

Elon Musk has been clear that governments are unlikely to regulate this in time. He is urging the major AI labs to cooperate, even at the cost of sharing access and intellectual property, and to self-regulate before the window closes. The risk is not abstract. It is more like a black-hole singularity appearing too close to where we live.

As someone who studies what is to come, I keep returning to the language of Revelation and “the mark of the beast.” Two things appear certain in that text: there will be a single global currency, and participation will not be optional for those who want to engage in ordinary commerce. When you examine why a unified currency is so powerful, the logic is hard to dismiss.

From the 9/11 Commission onward, one lesson has been consistent: evil is far harder to hide when money leaves a clear trail. Drug cartels, corrupt officials, and the illicit scam networks that now extract hundreds of billions of dollars a year would become dramatically more difficult to sustain if every transaction were visible and attributable.

Estimates suggest that somewhere between $2 and $6 trillion of the world’s commerce currently flows through illegal or quasi-illegal channels—not counting the more “legal” forms of corruption that operate through lobbying, regulatory capture, and loopholes. 

A single currency system, if it could be enforced, would not merely reduce crime. It would starve much of it. And if that system were tied to the physical person—the “mark on the flesh”—enforcement would become nearly total. 

But the bibles' last book "Revelation"  is unambiguous that such a system, once in place, will be accompanied by severe penalties for non-participation.

So the question is straightforward: if we are building systems that can, in principle, solve problems of this scale, does the capacity of a mature AI align with the mechanism described in that book? 

In many respects, it does. We are constructing tools that can track, predict, and enforce at a level no previous technology has approached.
That is real. 

At the same time, there is God, and there is a reality beyond what any intelligence—super or otherwise—can observe or measure from inside time and space. An AI can be an extraordinarily effective, unemotional problem-solver. 

What it cannot do is become the ground of meaning or the final authority. Any conformity it produces, however effective at suppressing certain forms of evil, will remain temporary and incomplete.

We are indeed entering a new age with Super Ai.  Ai will solve problems on a scale we have never seen before, faster than we can keep up with.  

Who would not elect to end criminal enterprise and corruption on a global scale?  ... but at what cost?

text:
For close to a decade I worked on how people and machines live alongside each other, first with human-machine interaction and autonomous systems at @volvocars and now at @MidbrainAI, and the thing that still bothers me most is how quickly our tools forget us.

I notice it in my own days all the time. I’ll talk an idea through out loud with a voice agent on a walk, sketch the layout on paper when words stop working, and then sit down in the evening and explain the whole thing again from scratch to a coding agent that has never heard of any of it. Each tool is impressive on its own, and yet every hop between them starts at zero.

My colleague Jesper Derehag just published a piece that puts words to what we’ve been building toward since 2024: a companion that carries one continuous thread of shared history through every tool you use, and keeps learning from it over years rather than hours.

The very important part is the distinction between storage and learning. Storing a fact like “user prefers tea” is useful, but it means the agent has to know to look for it, find it, and reason its way back to offering you tea every single time, which is both expensive and quietly fragile. 

A system that actually learns needs storage for exact recall and something closer to muscle memory for the things that happen often, so your preferences and habits simply become how the agent behaves.

That’s also where taste lives. I have never told an agent that I prefer short, friendly emails that end with a clear next step, but after months of small edits that is exactly what a learning companion should pick up on its own, the same way a colleague of many years just knows those nuances.

We started exploring this as a character in @Minecraft , then as a simulated human that helped robotics teams study how machines should behave around people, then in digital twins of entire cities, and today in coding agents. Every one of those embodiments taught us the same lesson: an agent only starts to feel useful once it has accumulated real experience with you and adapted to it.

And because that experience is so personal, we hold one principle firmly. Your agent’s memories, experiences and learned skills belong to you and no one else, which is also why, only half joking, we like to say that my agent is better than your agent.

如果美联储继续加息，试图强行将通胀压回 2%，可能最终把美国乃至全球经济拖入衰退。

text:
We fully support OpenAI's transparency initiative. Thanks to @merettm @markchen90 @gdb @sama for leading the way. 

We all got into this field to build safe AGI that is genuinely good for humanity. One of the hardest parts of AI safety is coordination, and this is a step in the right direction. Many more steps like this will be needed to deliver safe, contained, and aligned AGI in the next few years.

We're committed to sharing our pre-training progress on a common held-out evaluation set. With OpenAI's permission, we report MAI-2 Base on their evaluation set. Its log-perplexity is 0.819, putting it in the same ballpark as the GPT-5.6 Sol base model. Our model uses the same tokenizer as OpenAI, so the numbers are directly comparable. 

In the future, to be able to compare across labs we might need to report bits-per-byte (BPB) rather than perplexity since different labs use different tokenizers. We will also need different evaluation datasets - the fact we have access to OpenAI's evaluation dataset is a special case.

Safety and alignment is now the mission. It's the absolute number one most important focus for our industry. And it begins with small, practical steps like these towards better coordination on pacing.

text:
There are really two camps inside the crypto industry today:

1. Camp one continues to trade digital currencies (SOV, store-of-value coins) that have no cash flows and trade off flows and narratives like commodities. In fact, they are digital commodities.

2. The second camp is focused on cash-flowing businesses who have tokenized equity onchain, have revenues and cash flows which can be discounted at an appropriate discount rate and valued using intrinsic valuation (as opposed to the power of the imagination or memetics).

People will continue to speculate on digital commodities but the far more interesting opportunity on a 3-5 year timeframe (not that most people wait that long anyways, they want a million dollars yesterday) is the opportunity to own equity in some of the fastest-growing Wall Street businesses, which are currently being unbundled onchain. Hyperliquid did this with unregulated offshore derivatives (in fact, just perpetual futures), and a team of 11 people made billions in revenue and captured it with HYPE which is tokenized equity in the business.

This process is now being repeated with some of the largest businesses on Wall Street, unbeknownst to most because they don't have a background in capital markets, finance, or accounting, and would rather continue to trade their beloved internet coins. The notion that crypto is just store of value coins and speculation is a grossly reductive and deeply myopic point of view, often vocalized by people without the background or preparation to understand the TAM of what is coming.

It is not an exaggeration to say the unbundling of Wall Street and the rewriting of finance is at least 1,000x larger opportunity than the sum total of all of the speculation that is currently happening and the trading of all of these SoV coins combined.

text:
Approving browser access without transferring your keys is very powerful. So that a new browser shouldn’t need a copy of your private keys. 🔐

In the AgentKeys local development setup, the browser creates its own passkey and asks for access to your existing account. The request contains public information, so you can check which account, website and browser you’re approving. Your existing private keys aren’t copied into the browser.

🖥️ Approval and sign-in are two separate steps. You approve the request through the local command-line tool. Then the browser signs in with its own passkey. Having the request file isn’t enough to sign in, and this local setup doesn’t require an email account.

🏡 That’s how we want access to work for personal and family agents: adding another way to manage them shouldn’t mean handing over the keys to your account.

🛠️ We tested approval, sign-in and signing back in with a simulated authenticator in Chrome. Physical authenticators weren’t part of this test, and this isn’t a consumer rollout.

text:
Jensen Huang has stepped down as NVIDIA's CEO. Could his 33 years there turn out to be the groundwork for a second act? Morris Chang's story offers a striking precedent.

Chang left Texas Instruments in 1983 after 25 years. He had led its semiconductor business, then moved into a role farther from its core. After stints at General Instrument and Taiwan's Industrial Technology Research Institute, he founded TSMC in 1987, aged 55.

His idea opened a door for engineers who could design chips but could not afford a fab: TSMC would manufacture their designs without selling its own competing chips. As fabless companies emerged, that division of labor reshaped the industry.

NVIDIA was one of the companies that grew with TSMC's help. Around 1997, Huang wrote directly to Chang seeking manufacturing support. Chang called him back. By 2006, TSMC had produced 500 million NVIDIA processors.

Chang later recalled inviting Huang to become TSMC's CEO in 2013. Huang turned him down: he already had a job. When Chang asked again weeks later, the answer was the same.

For Huang, Chang's career offers more than an industry success story: decades of experience can become the foundation for a new business.

Elon Musk's proposed Terafab raises an intriguing possibility. The ambition is to bring chip design, manufacturing, memory and advanced packaging together to serve Tesla's autonomous driving, Optimus robots and SpaceX's computing needs.

Building the factory would be only the beginning. Producing chips at a workable cost, delivering them reliably and fitting them into a complete computing system would take deep experience. Huang has spent decades working across chip products, software and manufacturing partnerships.

If the two ever teamed up, their strengths could be complementary: Musk's demand for computing power and engineering resources, alongside Huang's product judgment and industry relationships.

The contrast with Chang is what makes the idea compelling. Chang separated chip design from manufacturing. Terafab aims to bring more of the chain together. Huang could again find himself at the center of a change in how the semiconductor industry works.

Chang was 55 when he founded TSMC. His example makes it easy to imagine another great venture ahead of Huang. He once declined Chang's job. One day, could he follow Chang's path?

#JensenHuang #TSMC #Semiconductors

quoted_text:
.@Starcloud_ was quoted $100M to build their first data center in space. They built it themselves for $2.5M.

That satellite put the first Nvidia H100 in space, 100x more GPU compute than anything done before.

And @PhilipJohnston thinks that's where all AI compute is eventually is going.

He walks me through why space will be the cheapest place to run AI, the physics behind operating a data center in space, why Nvidia invested even after one of their GPUs died, and the dynamic of competing with SpaceX while relying on their rockets to get up there.

We also get into what really happens in a tranched funding round, what @ycombinator is really backing, the importance of talent density and holding a high hiring bar, and his $15M probe to Alpha Centauri that won't arrive for 80,000 years.

text:
OpenAI 首席科学家 Jakub 发表了一篇倡议文「Perplexity and Intelligence」，行业应该用“对数困惑度”（log-perplexity）来反映了底层智能的进展，模型在预训练阶段就涌现出的能力，以免在 RL 阶段控制不住，因为模型的全部能力都是在这个阶段具备的。就像 Elon 补充的：只有预训练才是“训练”。如果你只做后训练，就像你打扮好去锻炼，然后直接洗澡，实际上根本没“锻炼”👀

从信息论来看，模型猜得越准，存这段文本需要的比特就越少，，平均损失 L 本身就是“每个词要用多少信息量来存”。这就是 llya 说的「压缩就是预测」：降低困惑度等于压缩得更好，压缩得更好等于抓到了更短、更本质的规律，也就是他那句「最短程序泛化最好」。

GPT-3.5 的对数困惑度约 0.99，困惑度 e0.99～2.7，平均每个词在大约 2.7 个选项之间犹豫；现在内部用的模型约0.73，困惑度约 2.08。Jakub 说的“越接近底线，困惑度的进步越小，但对应智力飞跃越大”。至于底线：数据本身就有随机性，比如注释里人随手写的话，谁也不可能百分之百猜中，所以对数困惑度不可能降到 0 。。。

在 @Tz_2022 同学的启发下，用 Gemini Neon 对 Jakub 文章中的“困惑度”坐标图做了个推演，随着模型逼近那个未知的熵下限 H0，曲线的下降斜率会逐渐放缓，但“单位困惑度下降”换来的智能跃迁会越来越大——越往后，哪怕再压低 0.01，都意味着模型吃透了更深层的规律。

- 0.65 ～ 0.55：若 AI 加速预训练研发兑现，能力会从“攻克单个数学/网安难题”扩展到端到端跨学科自主科研——在生物医药、材料、物理、芯片架构等领域自主提出假设、设计实验并迭代理论，人类研究员的角色进一步转向目标设定与物理验证。

- 接近 0.4 (熵下限 H0)：曲线明显变平，但模型已逼近静态语料的 Bayes 最优压缩器，几乎穷尽人类已有知识与代码中的全部可压缩规律。此时瓶颈不再是“预训练降困惑度”，而是真实世界物理实验速度、算力/能源上限与长程行动闭环。

- 如果突破熵墙：将实现传说中的心理史学与脑机直连，我们将可以毫秒级推演全球经济、气候与文明演化分支，直接解码生物神经网络，实现意识带宽扩容 。。。

但就像绝大多数科学家的共识，我们这个宇宙是不会让这个数值等于零的，信息的传输无法超越光速，P 也不会等于 NP 🤔

text:
~546 ETH just got locked in Blur Pool forever. 

Blur Pool is a nonstandard ERC20: it has no transfer() and no approve(). The only way to turn BlurPool ETH into regular ETH is to use `withdraw()`, which several contracts holding BlurPool (from royalties) do not implement. The only escape hatch for them was for Blur to upgrade the pool contract. Or at least, that WAS the only escape hatch.

Blur just executed a series of transactions to brick the Safe that owns Blur, Blend, and BlurPool. That means that finally, officially, Blur can never be upgraded.

I went through the ~125k Blur Pool holders. 889 of those are contracts, holding 1,216 ETH.

315 of those contracts are immutable and do not implement a `withdraw()`, and they hold a total of 545.6 ETH. There is no way for them to ever receive the ETH.

558 contracts hold 550.9 ETH that IS withdrawable, but hasn't been withdrawn yet.

2 contracts owned by Cool Cats owns 117.1 ETH and are unverified, but through decompilation I was able to uncover a generic fallback function that appears to be able to withdraw if passed the correct calldata.

Out of the locked ETH, the biggest locked bags:

• Moonbirds family (PROOF): 173.2 ETH. 
• Milady "One" vault: 85.0 ETH.
• 0xSplits SplitWallets: 82.6 ETH across 63 splits.
• Super PUMA 0x41197b…: 62.9 ETH. 
• Invisible Friends 26.5, Iron Paw Gang 21.2, loomlock 16, then a long tail of royalty splitters under 2 ETH each.

The lesson here is that royalty splitters, simple as they may seem, need to be equipped to handle the unexpected. Either a generic extcall or upgradeability are good solutions, of course with appropriate safety considerations.

Anyway, RIP blur. you will not be missed.

Bloomberg: Self-powered data centers ("behind-the-meter") are mostly still plans:

developers have announced about 90GW of their own power plants for US data centers ("behind-the-meter"), but only about 2GW of that, around 2%, actually runs so far.

The grid keeps power flowing when one machine fails because it draws on many plants and lines, while a single on-site plant has no such backup. 
AI workloads also swing demand within seconds, enough to damage some on-site generators, and solar plus batteries would need almost 1,800 hectares to run a 100MW Texas data center just 98% of the year. 

So developers build extra gas capacity, pay over $100 per megawatt-hour against about $90 for grid power, and mostly treat their own plants as a bridge until the grid connection arrives.

text:
a self-guaranteeing promise is

1. verifiable: it's easy for someone to test
2. non-reversible: it can't be taken back
author: kepano
quoted_text:
Self-guaranteeing promises

Companies break promises all the time. A self-guaranteeing promise does not require you to trust anyone. You can verify a self-guaranteeing promise yourself.

File over app is a self-guaranteeing promise. If files are in your control, in an open format, you can use those files in another app at any time. Not an export. The exact same files. It’s good practice to test this with any self-proclaimed file-over-app app you use.

Terms and policies are not self-guaranteeing. A company may promise the privacy of your data, but those policies can change at any time. Changes can retroactively affect data you have spent years putting into the tool. A self-guaranteeing promise about privacy gives you proof that the tool cannot access your data in the first place. Examples: Google, Zoom, Dropbox, Tumblr, Slack, Adobe, Figma (see links).

Encoding values into a governance structure is not self-guaranteeing. Given enough motivation, the corporate structure can be reversed. The structure is not in your hands. Example: OpenAI.

Open source alone is not self-guaranteeing. Even open source apps can rely on data that is stuck in databases or in proprietary formats that are difficult to switch away from. Open source is not a reliable safeguard against the biases of venture capital. Examples: Omnivore, Skiff.

When you choose to use a tool, the future of that tool is always ambiguous. On a long enough timeline the substrate changes. Your needs change, the underlying operating system changes, the company goes out of business or gets acquired, better options come along.

It is possible to accept the ambiguousness of a tool's future if you choose tools that make self-guaranteeing promises.

author: DashHuang
quoted_text:
In case anyone is curious:

We’ve had a ~pixel-perfect world model since last year, which is critical for synthetic data generation. 

The (much) smaller version of that in the car is a conditional mean-flow model, based on the recent sequence of Tesla Universal Vision Encoder features, which are the same ones that are plugged into the 3B encoder model that produces the driving actions. 

We fork off from these UVE features, then run a separate ~1B diffusion model. This takes in the previous reality-view generation with added noise and then denoises it to the current visualization. 

It then produces a small video chunk (8 images at 36 fps, at the resolution of the UI screen). This work is done by 1/2 of a TRIP engine every UVE frame at 18 hz and is spread over 4 cycles. 

Currently, the latency is a bit high due to compute constraints, but we have ways to interleave newer UVE features along the diffusion transformer layers to cut roughly 35% of the latency.

author: elonmusk
quoted_text:
In case anyone is curious:

We’ve had a ~pixel-perfect world model since last year, which is critical for synthetic data generation. 

The (much) smaller version of that in the car is a conditional mean-flow model, based on the recent sequence of Tesla Universal Vision Encoder features, which are the same ones that are plugged into the 3B encoder model that produces the driving actions. 

We fork off from these UVE features, then run a separate ~1B diffusion model. This takes in the previous reality-view generation with added noise and then denoises it to the current visualization. 

It then produces a small video chunk (8 images at 36 fps, at the resolution of the UI screen). This work is done by 1/2 of a TRIP engine every UVE frame at 18 hz and is spread over 4 cycles. 

Currently, the latency is a bit high due to compute constraints, but we have ways to interleave newer UVE features along the diffusion transformer layers to cut roughly 35% of the latency.

quoted_text:
We fully support OpenAI's transparency initiative. Thanks to @merettm @markchen90 @gdb @sama for leading the way. 

We all got into this field to build safe AGI that is genuinely good for humanity. One of the hardest parts of AI safety is coordination, and this is a step in the right direction. Many more steps like this will be needed to deliver safe, contained, and aligned AGI in the next few years.

We're committed to sharing our pre-training progress on a common held-out evaluation set. With OpenAI's permission, we report MAI-2 Base on their evaluation set. Its log-perplexity is 0.819, putting it in the same ballpark as the GPT-5.6 Sol base model. Our model uses the same tokenizer as OpenAI, so the numbers are directly comparable. 

In the future, to be able to compare across labs we might need to report bits-per-byte (BPB) rather than perplexity since different labs use different tokenizers. We will also need different evaluation datasets - the fact we have access to OpenAI's evaluation dataset is a special case.

Safety and alignment is now the mission. It's the absolute number one most important focus for our industry. And it begins with small, practical steps like these towards better coordination on pacing.

text:
To elaborate - 

If P = NP is proven & we get a practical polynomial-time algo for an NP-complete problem, modern cryptography largely collapses.

Most public-key systems (RSA, elliptic curves, Diffie-Hellman) rely on the hardness of problems that would suddenly become efficiently solvable. TLS, banking, digital signatures, secure messaging, and most of blockchain infra would become insecure unless built differently. Society would need an emergency global transition to new foundations - only info-theoretically secure methods (one-time pads) or certain quantum schemes would remain safe by default.

The upside is enormous: optimal solutions for logistics, scheduling, protein folding, circuit design, and countless optimization problems become feasible. But “polynomial time” can still be useless in practice if the degree or constants are huge, and a non-constructive proof would change almost nothing on its own.

But yeah - god help us if proven true.

text:
Lots of noise on here. A few things that should perhaps be more obvious than they are.
(1) The Lean-formalized proof of the Riemann hypothesis is exceedingly likely to be correct.
(2) No human understands it yet. There doesn't seem to be a meaningful obstruction to humans understanding it, though, and there's already a lot of activity in this direction.
(3) There are several competing claims by humans to have an alternate proof, or to have debunked the proof elicited from Claude by Alpöge. None of these claims seem to me to be credible. If something useful comes out of a claimed alternate proof that would be great of course.
(4) There's a huge amount of work to be done. Even for RH, there's a version of it for any system of polynomial equations, where in general we don't even know the relevant L-function converges on the critical line. RH is the case where the system of polynomials is empty.

text:
美联储一直坚持的 2%的通胀目标，其实也就是脑子一热，拍脑袋定下来的

1988年，新西兰财政部长 Roger Douglas 在电视采访中提出，希望把通胀降到0%—1%左右。

随后央行考虑到物价统计误差等因素，将目标调整为0%—2%，并在1990年正式写入政策协议。

加拿大、英国随后陆续采用通胀目标制，这套制度逐渐影响全球央行。

美国其实更晚。

1996年，美联储内部就2%目标展开过讨论，格林斯潘倾向于接近零的真实通胀，耶伦则支持保留适度通胀。

直到2012年，伯南克领导的美联储才正式确立以PCE衡量的2%长期通胀目标。

为什么是2%？

因为零通胀容易碰到工资难以下调、利率降息空间不足等问题，适度通胀能给经济调整留出余地。

所以2%从来不是经济学定律，它本质上是历史经验、政策妥协和市场预期共同形成的结果。

如果美联储继续坚持2%的目标，那接下来加息的话可能真的会出问题，单看SpaceX的担保融资利率已经达到8.259%，如果美联储继续加息，强行把通胀压回2%，可能把美国经济推入衰退。

The cost of equity capital has also increased materially with the recent substantial decline in the stock market. 

The Fed’s 2% inflation ambition is misguided. Geopolitical risk and the required investment in global military spending, de globalization and tariffs, and the massive AI infrastructure and related energy investment are features of the world that did not exist when the 2% target was set. 3% inflation is a more realistic ambition in the new world.

text:
历史上美股恐慌贪婪指数跌到9进入极度恐慌区间后美股会怎么走？上周五美股值得看的一个数据就是CNN恐慌贪婪指数跌到9的进入极度恐慌区间，印象中去年关税战指数跌倒3是过去这么多年恐贪指数一个极值。让GPT做了一个统计自2011年以来，美股共有136个交易日恐惧贪婪指数低于10，构成40段连续信号。把密集出现的信号合并成17轮行情，除去刚触发的本轮，已走完的 16 轮里：7 轮快速V 反，5轮反弹后二探或破底，4 轮继续下跌延后见底。尽管如此，16轮中有14轮在第21个交易日收涨。 

这次最值得对照的是2025年11月和2018年四季度：
1）前者说明AI估值担忧遇上货币政策预期改善，可以很快止跌；
2）后者说明一旦风险从股票估值传向盈利和融资成本即使出现强反弹，也可能要回头再二探一次。

本轮已经出现了值得跟踪的信用市场证据。上周五CNN七个分项中，标普动量只有0.2，避险需求0.8，波动率分项 1.32，期权分项2.0，短期避险已经相当集中。与此同时，美国高收益债利差从 11/13 的323个基点扩大到11/19的 
352个基点。到 11/20，投资级信用违约互换指数CDX IG的利差盘中一度达到 65.5个基点，为 3月底以来最高。高收益债数据截至周四，CDX 是周五盘中读数，两者都指向融资风险开始被重新定价。

所以反弹时信用利差怎么走来区分这两个历史参照：
1）如果纳指反弹、科技债和广义信用利差同步收窄，更接近2025 年11月的快速稳定；
2）如果纳指大涨几天，信用保护成本却继续上升，2018年四季度的经验就更有参考价值。

所以整体上：
市场进入极度恐慌区间，短线反弹是大概率的，是直接V反还是二探甚至延后见底还要再看。这一次个人更倾向会有二探或者延后见底，核心还是宏观和产业政策都还没明朗（上周推文聊到市场未来走出来要看宏观产业的三个层面，见引用推文最后部分），如果之后真能出现如去年10月恐慌贪婪指数被打倒5以下，市场恐慌到无以复加，那可能真是绝佳机会。

得克萨斯：参议院和州长双翻盘（州长是1990年代以来民主党首次）。
堪萨斯参议院：1932年以来首次民主党胜利。
南卡罗来纳、密西西比、爱荷华、俄亥俄等也出现翻盘，这已经不是边缘波动，而是广泛支持流失。
4）州一级
（1）民主党净增约6个州长席（包括佐治亚、爱荷华、内华达、俄亥俄、得克萨斯、阿拉斯加等），民主党获得多数州长席位（约30-20）。
（2）多个议院翻盘，民主党新增多个“三权合一”（州长+两院）
共和党几乎没有成功翻转任何民主党控制的参议院席位
本次中期选举投票率约49%，民，是1914年以来第二高中期投票率（仅次于2018年）。即使共和党进行了中期重划选区、也遭遇了大败。

两院失守且席位被大幅拉开、14点普选票优势 、深层红州翻盘 、州长与州议会大面积失利，这些都指向了这是近几十年最严重一次中期选举失败。选举结果刚出来的时候，我是远远低估这次失败的严重程度，以及惨败之后的一系列连锁反应。

2、惨败的连锁反应
1）最直接的就是川普在共和党的威信与影响力被极大的削弱
之前川普可以依靠自己的威望和影响力，死死压住党内的不同意见，其他声音都不能完全冒头。但这次惨败趟则让川普的影响力大打折扣，通胀民生和AI发展数据中心建设潮的负面声音就被放大，因为这是惨败的直接原因、因为都败成这样了、川普也不能不承认。

之前共和党内的政治人物都需要川普背书，但现在的问题是背书效应已经大打折扣、24年川普背书的议员赢得大选概率是89%，现在已经不到50%，川普背书已经不是助力而是阻力了，那么共和党内持不同主张的政治人物都开始活跃并强硬起来。

2）“倒黄”事件就是川普威望和影响力被削弱的直接连锁反应之一。
现在大家都清楚，这次“倒黄”主力不是民主党，而是共和党内对华强硬派，卢比奥、贝森特还有共和党国会几个委员会主席。之前他们可都不敢忤逆川普的意愿，但是这次即使川普再三帮助老黄发声，但效果甚微。

老黄离开市场自然对英伟达的未来很悲观、技术迭代速度可能放缓、产业生态支持力度也会大幅减弱。这些都让担忧一步步加强

3）产业政策的大逆转
民主党不仅大幅度领先优势拿下国会多数席位、现在还有三十个州长位子，那么市场就会但心川普过去两年积极推动的AI和加密的产业政策会被逆转：
AI监管会更加严格、AI基建会大幅放缓；
加密立法几无可能、加密清算更加猛烈；
这种预期的改变，对无论是对冲基金和长线资金信心的影响和动摇是巨大的，所以我们看到的没顾上对冲基金在大幅度砍仓，然后长线资金也是不断减持仓位。
币市则表现为中期选举后比特币ETF连日大额净流出、稳定币发行量持续下降。

4）然后就是美联储官员的激进表态
你看川普影响力一被削弱、FOMC票委们的表态就大胆起来，这里典型就是沃勒、之前还算是鸽派、现在已经完全转变成了强鹰派，连12月50个基点的加息论调都提出来了，多名票委的鹰派发言，自然也让市场对12月以及明年初的利率走势更加悲观。

当然核心也是现在美伊博弈在中期选举还没有明确的说法，市场也很担心通胀的走势。

可以看到“倒黄”事件，产业政策被逆转的担忧、联储官员的鹰派很大程度上都是这次中选共和党惨败带来的连锁反应，一系列悲观情景下资金也是连锁踩踏，最后也止不住连锁出清，是市场大跌底层逻辑。

3、接下来怎么看？
看配图2，也是周三在币安广场AMA里聊到的三个变量：
1）油价/通胀走势决定联储利率走向；
2）新政治生态下AI政策比当下市场预期的要更收紧和会略缓和些；
3）AI商业化是不是继续处于加速状态；

当然从个人角度核心是前两者、第三点当下看还是处于加速之中。

从另一个角度看市场一方面是对产业政策逆转和党争做悲观的定价、另一方面也是“死给你看”倒逼两党表态、特别是民主党到底要对AI政策逆转到什么程度？资金看不清、只能做悲观定价但说最悲观还要再看

text: A $2 million exploit leads to a $3.7 million free-for-all as traders empty Fusionist’s ACE bridge
author: cryptounfolded

text:
Fusionist’s ACE bridge drained after privileged minter exploit on BNB Chain. Attacker minted quintillions of unbacked tokens, sold for ~$1.87–2M USDT (laundered via Tornado Cash), crashing the price. Traders then bridged the fakes to claim 53.7M real ACE (~$3.7M) from reserves, leaving the bridge empty. Pre-exploit supply was ~116M.

ACE fell 8–13% (MCAP ~$8–9M); project paused BNB transfers/trading/bridging. Gate rolling back trades; some users profited heavily on OKX. 

Takeaway: Privileged roles enabled the mint; opportunistic extraction amplified losses to ~$4M total. Classic bridge centralization risk with no clear recovery path yet.

They just think that these are JPEGs used as wrapper for tokens that you buy & sell onchain and they’re trackable onchain

text:
We fully support OpenAI's transparency initiative. Thanks to @merettm @markchen90 @gdb @sama for leading the way. 

We all got into this field to build safe AGI that is genuinely good for humanity. One of the hardest parts of AI safety is coordination, and this is a step in the right direction. Many more steps like this will be needed to deliver safe, contained, and aligned AGI in the next few years.

We're committed to sharing our pre-training progress on a common held-out evaluation set. With OpenAI's permission, we report MAI-2 Base on their evaluation set. Its log-perplexity is 0.819, putting it in the same ballpark as the GPT-5.6 Sol base model. Our model uses the same tokenizer as OpenAI, so the numbers are directly comparable. 

In the future, to be able to compare across labs we might need to report bits-per-byte (BPB) rather than perplexity since different labs use different tokenizers. We will also need different evaluation datasets - the fact we have access to OpenAI's evaluation dataset is a special case.

Safety and alignment is now the mission. It's the absolute number one most important focus for our industry. And it begins with small, practical steps like these towards better coordination on pacing.

我准备重新做一个自己的harness，把自己日常的一些工作任务都装进去。

最近发现Grok Bot虽然工具好用，但后面的模型不太行，回复内容压缩太厉害，而且经常跟GPT一样叨叨，反面的话说了又说，这不是…不是…，烦死我了。

我觉得日常最好用的模型还是Opus 5.5，给它一个任务，多数情况下都可以One Shot来解决。当然，目前一个问题是有点太慢，跑个任务经常几十分钟出去了，不如Sol干活爽快。

但从Harness角度，无论是Codex、Claude Code，还是Alma，感觉都很难完全满足我的需求。比如Alma也是一个session、一个session去启动，如果我想建一个长久的Agent，或实现主Agent和子Agent之间沟通的话，好像不太支持。

我感觉还是Grok Bot这种形态会更适合我这种非开发背景的同学。它的记忆和上下文管理做得不错，临时启动和调用Agent也很方便。

所以我准备搭一个自己的harness试试了，把自己的一些常用任务全都包进去。后续有成果我分享出来。

author: sleepy0x13
quoted_text:
Chamath Predicts the Rise of AI’s Magnificent 10: “Dirt to Application”

“I think there are going to be 9-10 mega corps that get built over the next decade because of AI. And I think that each mega corp is going to go from the application layer all the way down to the dirt.

Now, why do I say this? I think the deal that Palo Alto Networks did yesterday rips the Band-Aid off, and I think was very smart.

Why were they rewarded yesterday? The stock was up 8 or 9% at one point for buying an AI company, and Nikesh said it in the press release, he's like, ‘This is us venturing outside of security, our first big venture,’ and the market was like, ‘Thank God.’

And so what's happening?

He's going to own the model. Then he's going to eventually own the dirt and the land and have the data centers vertically integrated. Then he's going to go up the stack to applications.

What is Anthropic doing? ANT, with all their money, they're already going down to the dirt, and they're going up to the application stack. OpenAI is doing the same thing. SpaceX is doing the same thing.

So I think what AI is creating essentially is haves and have-nots. The haves are the folks that have these critical assets that can be very tightly vertically integrated, and I think that there's going to be 7-10 of these folks.

So I think if you view it that way, you're going to see these 8, 9, 10 conglomerates, and now the market is betting who is a conglomerate and who is not.

And that more than anything, I think, explains the flows over the last few weeks and probably the last year, even.”

text:
can you hedge onchain costs the way airlines hedge fuel?

tested it on six years of data.

every crypto business pays costs it doesn't control: borrow rates, perp funding, gas.

the tools to hedge them today don't fit:
→ perps can liquidate you
→ options need a volatility market that doesn't exist for these rates
→ prediction markets pay $1 or $0, which you can't size to a bill

so i tested a simpler shape: a capped hedge.

1/ you pick a level
2/ if the 30-day average goes above it, you get paid the difference, up to a limit
3/ paid automatically in usdc
4/ every payout is fully funded onchain up front. no margin, no liquidation

what i found

for buyers: costs a little more in a normal month, cuts the bad ones.

ethereum gas:
> worst month: $3,845 → $2,195
> month-to-month swings: $820 → $180

for the pool: it paid.

usdc borrow rates, 2020–2026:
> $2.72m a year in premiums
> $0.24m in claims
> no losing year. even 2023, the worst, held

what's still broken
→ prices run 3–10x actual claims, because the model leans on the past year
→ funding rates keep moving once they start, which gives buyers an edge over the pool

those are the next problems i'm solving.

tradfi has had this for decades, behind paperwork and $1m minimums.

onchain it can start at $100.

黄乐事件的背后竟然涉及柬埔寨太子集团

金融时报近日追查英伟达芯片如何流入中国，查到了柬埔寨太子集团。由黄乐掌管的公司负责购买芯片，而胡小伟则被指将部分芯片运进中国。

那么黄乐是怎么和胡小伟有关联的呢？

2023 年黄乐买下第七大道的新加坡子公司，改名叫 Megaspeed，可能很多小伙伴不知道，当初第七大道有一款叫弹弹堂的游戏在海外非常火爆，其中 FaceBook 就是一个庞大的分销平台，我在做游戏的时候还拿到过 FB 上弹弹堂的运营权，那时候可真的是印钞机。

当时的胡小伟在一家宁夏公司当董事，这家公司的多数股权当时握在世纪华通董事长王佶手里。所以通过第七大道黄乐和胡小伟就搭上了关系。

2024年底到2025年底的一年中，Megaspeed 的马来西亚子公司从服务器供应商 Aivres 进口高达 46 亿美元的英伟达芯片，这部分芯片中有部分进入了中国市场，而胡小伟就是运输进入中国的参与者。

美国财政部今年 6 月的制裁公告称，胡小伟被视为太子集团的二号人物，曾替集团管理柬埔寨以外的公司。目前太子集团否认胡小伟为其工作，也否认参与走私。

美国司法部目前正在对 Megaspeed 展开刑事调查。

text:
Hoy quiero hablarles de tres héroes salvadoreños que perdieron la vida mientras cumplían una misión lejos de nuestra patria.

Tres miembros de nuestra Fuerza Armada que viajaron a Haití con un propósito: rescatar a cuatro de sus compañeros que habían sido secuestrados por pandillas haitianas.

Lamentablemente, una explosión accidental durante esa misión les arrebató la vida.

Sus nombres son: el teniente Cristian Daniel Palacios Santos, el cabo Emerson Alexander Zepeda Zelada y el cabo Wilber Manuel Serrano Medina.

Conocí de primera mano la valentía del teniente Palacios Santos. Durante un operativo, en un momento crítico en el que unos contratistas privados abandonaron sus posiciones, el teniente tomó el control de la situación y actuó con rapidez y determinación, logrando salvar varias vidas, entre ellas las de sus propios compañeros.

Todos aplaudimos su valentía.

Recuerdo que en ese momento pensé: “Este muchacho llegará lejos. Tiene todo el temple y la capacidad de un líder”. Jamás imaginé que, poco tiempo después, estaría entre los fallecidos en un accidente.

También me informaron del extraordinario valor de los cabos Zepeda Zelada y Serrano Medina. Durante unas pruebas en El Salvador, una granada quedó atorada en un dron. La batería estaba por agotarse y no era posible dirigirlo hacia una zona completamente segura para que se estrellara. Serrano Medina sostuvo el dron a aproximadamente un metro y medio del suelo mientras Zepeda Zelada desactivaba manualmente la granada.

Sabían perfectamente el inmenso riesgo que estaban corriendo, pero aun así decidieron actuar para proteger a los demás.

Y lo lograron.

Estas no son simplemente historias sobre tres héroes. Son acciones que nos permiten entender quiénes eran estos hombres: militares capaces, valientes y comprometidos con una misión que siempre pusieron por encima de su propia seguridad.

Varias veces he dicho que siempre he admirado a las personas que deciden dedicar sus vidas a salvar las de otros. Porque hay algo extraordinario en ellas. Algo que no es natural, que no es común, que no es normal.

Todos los seres humanos tenemos una reacción instintiva ante el peligro. Si vemos un peligro, huimos de él. Si hay un incendio, corremos y tratamos de alejarnos. Pero un bombero no huye del incendio, hace lo contrario, lo que casi nadie más haría, y en lugar de huir del incendio, corre hacia él, arriesga su vida, camina entre las llamas si es necesario para salvar a los demás.

Eso no es algo normal, es algo extraordinario.

Si escuchamos una balacera, nuestro instinto es huir de los disparos, buscar refugio, mantenernos alejados. Pero un policía hace lo contrario. Ellos no huyen de los disparos como haríamos todos, van hacia ellos, sacan su pistola y corren hacia el peligro para salvar a los que están en él.

Eso no es algo normal, es algo extraordinario.

Lo vimos con los rescatistas que enviamos a Venezuela, salvadoreños abriendo túneles en estructuras inestables que podrían colapsar en cualquier momento. Nuestro instinto natural es huir de un edificio que se desmorona, pero nuestros rescatistas hacían lo contrario: entraban a esas estructuras, sabiendo que podían morir ahí adentro, para salvar a quienes estaban atrapados.

Eso no lo haría casi nadie, mucho menos por un desconocido, pero ellos sí, porque los rescatistas, al igual que los policías, bomberos y militares, reaccionan de una manera totalmente diferente a todos los demás. Ellos no huyen del peligro, van hacia él. Eso es difícil de entender para la gente normal, pero ellos no son gente normal, son gente extraordinaria.

Cuando los demás retroceden, ellos avanzan. Sabiendo perfectamente que eso puede costarles la vida misma.

Y no es que no tengan miedo, es que hay algo más fuerte que ese miedo: su deseo de salvar a los demás.

Esa es la vocación que mueve a nuestros militares, a nuestros policías, bomberos y rescatistas. Personas que han decidido dedicar sus vidas a proteger la de los demás…
author: nayibbukele

text:
Y hoy honramos a tres de esos hombres que perdieron su vida en nuestra misión de rescate.

Tres salvadoreños que demostraron, con sus acciones, el verdadero significado del valor, del deber y de la lealtad hacia sus compañeros.

A sus familias quiero decirles algo: El Salvador reconoce a sus seres queridos como héroes. Su sacrificio no será olvidado y ustedes no estarán solos.

Vamos a acompañarlos y apoyarlos en todo lo que necesiten.

He creado un fondo de un millón de dólares para estas tres familias. 200,000 dólares que serán entregados inmediatamente a cada una de ellas, y el resto para garantizarles un ingreso mensual. Esto aparte de las prestaciones de ley que recibirán de parte de la Fuerza Armada.

Sé perfectamente que ninguna cantidad de dinero puede compensar la pérdida de un ser querido. No existe nada que pueda llenar ese vacío, el único consuelo solo puede venir de Dios y es en Él en el que debemos buscar refugio en momentos de dolor.

Pero queremos que sepan que su país está agradecido y que, en medio de este dolor, no tendrán que enfrentar solos estas dificultades.

A todos los miembros de nuestra Fuerza Armada desplegados en esta misión de rescate, quiero decirles que conozco los riesgos que enfrentan y admiro profundamente la valentía y la determinación con la que continúan cumpliendo su deber. Como se les dijo en un inicio, quienes decidan regresar pueden hacerlo de inmediato, sin temor a represalias y sin temor de que su regreso ponga en riesgo la misión, ya que muchos de sus compañeros se han ofrecido para relevar a quien desee ser relevado.

Sé que han perdido a tres compañeros. Como comandante general de la Fuerza Armada, yo he perdido también a tres de los míos. Sé que su ausencia se siente y que esta tragedia nos ha golpeado profundamente.

Pero también sé que ellos siguen vivos en cada uno de nosotros.

Que Dios bendiga, dé fortaleza y consuelo a las familias del teniente Cristian Daniel Palacios Santos, del cabo Emerson Alexander Zepeda Zelada y del cabo Wilber Manuel Serrano Medina.

Y que Dios Todopoderoso proteja a toda nuestra tropa desplegada en Haití.

"Trade for long enough, and you discover that the market has a godlike ability to peer into your soul, learn your character flaws, your private fears, weaknesses, pain thresholds. And the market uses this knowledge to tease you, sometimes letting you get away with recklessness, rewarding your greed, luring you to commit more brazen sins. At other times it creates false hope that you’ll escape whatever predicament you’ve gotten yourself into, allowing you to believe your own lies, letting you imagine you’ll slip its grasp this one time. Just like it did to leveraged Nvidia longs this Tuesday evening, when a blowout earnings report lifted the stock sharply higher after hours. By Friday's close it had lost 23% on the week. The process wears you down, so that at your weakest moment you puke positions at the absolute low, knowing it’s almost certainly a mistake, but grateful to end the torture. And breathe again.

When enough people hold the same view and pair it with arrogance, the market rounds up the herd and culls it in a violent flush. One man’s stop loss pushes price lower to the next man’s point of maximum pain, a runaway wildfire, a scorched earth cleanse. Sodom. Gomorrah. Like in February 2018, when the sellers of equity volatility watched their hallowed inverse VIX products lose 96% of their value in a ferocious afternoon. There was no specific catalyst. No real reason. Just the market gods at work. And it’s the very personal struggle with this omniscient superintelligence that makes those of us who have survived more introspective and humbler with time. It keeps us on the lookout for those moments when the herd has been rounded up and is being led to slaughter. Doing everything in our power to avoid that fate, and to capitalize on the chaos."

Eric Peters, One River Asset Management

After 12 years, I'm moving my money back to TradFi...

For the past ~7 months, I've been moving a ton of money from onchain to tradfi. Money I never ever thought I would have a reason to move to tradfi, money that, in one form or another, has been onchain since I bought my first BTC back in 2014.

It's been a painfully tedious process bridging it. (I might write about that some other day, but that's not the point of this post.)

About 8 months ago, I came to the conclusion that having substantial amounts of capital parked onchain wasn't worth the r/r anymore, for several reasons...

BTC is not a SoV, and I haven't held it in a while. 
Stables are nowhere near as decentralized as we pretend they are. 
DeFi's third-party and smart-contract risks relative to the yields you get are a kick in the nuts.

I could go on...
 
I've been putting up with all of this for years because I really didn't want to go through the process of moving all that money to tradfi.

And because, despite all those problems, I had always considered onchain superior to tradfi.... Particularly in terms of portability + permissionless access + self-custody, which made putting up with all the other bullshit worth it.

But having been at the frontier of AI since day one, and watching how quickly these models have advanced in mathematical reasoning and automated vulnerability discovery, I've become extremely concerned about the security assumptions that hold this entire onchain machine together.

With the most fundamental one being cryptographic risk. AI can't break Bitcoin's elliptic-curve cryptography today, and quantum computing is a whole different beast. But imagine a future breakthrough that makes deriving private keys from exposed public keys computationally feasible....Imagine waking up to Satoshi's coins moving because someone had managed to reconstruct his private keys.....Imagine what that would do to confidence in every other wallet secured by the same cryptographic assumptions.

We have built an enormous financial machine on top of cryptographic primitives + software implementations +  security assumptions that have held up remarkably well so far.....But the amount of intelligence and computational effort that can be directed toward finding weaknesses in that machine is changing very damn fast.

And I have no interest in finding out which part breaks first with a substantial amount of money sitting inside it.

At this point, I'm more convinced than ever that some version of this is a question of WHEN, rather than IF. 

I have no idea when, and I might bevery wrong about the tl, but the potential loss is too large relative to what I'm being compensated to keep that capital onchain.

Now.....I'm sure that if I leave it here, one of the first and most popular comments will be something along the lines of:

"You're a fucking idiot. If cryptography breaks and crypto goes down, the entire financial system goes down with it."

And yes, that's absolutely right, given that Tradfi depends on cryptography too.

But here's my thinking...

I'd rather be fucked alongside the rest of the world than exclusively alongside magic internet money enjoyors.

Because when the world's financial system gets fucked, it's in EVERYONE's interest to fix it. Governments, central banks, financial institutions, you name it... The entire world's machinery will be put to work to get shit back in order.

Not so much the case for onchain....

If some critical piece of onchain infrastructure breaks who tf is coming to save us?

Nobody owes us shit.... And if the rest of the financial system is also compromised, you can bet nobody is going to waste resources saving our magic internet money while trying to save the rest of the world.

So I'd rather have that money on the other side.

And if a large portion of your NW is sitting onchain, I'd suggest you consider taking that hedge too.

PS: This doesn't mean I'll stop trading onchain or being active in crypto...Ofc I won't....I love this weird fkn world too much.... 

But going forward, I'll only keep the money I'm actively playing with onchain, and not a cent more.

深圳 APEC 是不是把美国人的什么开关给碰着了？怎么一回华盛顿，连刚说过的狠话都开始往回收了。

最抽象的是美国财长贝森特。

11 月 15 日，他还在炮轰英伟达，质疑公司为了赚钱违规向中国出售芯片，要求董事会必须从外部找新 CEO。

到了 11 月 22 日，CBS 记者追问：你不是要求英伟达找外部 CEO 吗？特朗普却希望黄仁勋复职，你们到底听谁的？

贝森特的回答简直绝了：

「黄仁勋现在不就是外部人士吗？」

text:
7) Related to point 6, and I’m admittedly a ceaseless clanging gong on this issue, the Senate prioritizes the comfort of senators over and above the actual job. Voting late, voting on Fridays, grinding out procedural processes, it’s just too much for them. A lot of them will just leave. They prioritize everything else but the actual job and then demand voters take them seriously when they don’t even take themselves seriously.

In that sense it’s easier to tweet about “what could have been” then to own the fact that you sometimes have to be the guy that makes it real. (Because one senator usually can. They really are power centers in their own right.)

8) Finally, there is the death by a thousand cuts theory. The Senate is actually made to solve problems and that function is pushed along by the institution being a relational body. SO MANY issues used to be solved by senators talking to each other during votes or on the subway or just wandering into each other’s offices or during the conferences lunches.

Now votes are 60+ mins so senators never see each other. The conference lunches are scripted or have outside speakers and never allow for discussion. Senators work 2.5 days a week. Staff work from home or never leave their offices so never meet each other. There isn’t an amendment process to sharpen engagement and negotiation skills. And senators just tweet at each other instead of working out their issues face to face.

Can the Senate be fixed? I think it can be. But rules changes or nuking the filibuster or firing the parliamentarian aren’t going to do it. This isn’t a mechanical problem. It’s a problem of will and desire.

The Senate has a Leader but what it currently lacks is leaders of men.

text:
I have so many theories as to why this is. 

1) A learned helplessness in the rank and file, instituted over the past two decades by a bipartisan leadership style that dictated to members in a top down manner what they were going to do and enforced it punitively using campaign cash, committee seats, etc, as leverage. 

2) At least on the R side, we have reached a critical mass of senators who have never seen a functioning Senate. They have no idea how powerful they actually are or how the Senate operated in the Before Times (not even that long ago! Like in the 90s and early 2000s!).

Current senators either don’t want to know and outsource that knowledge to staff who are disinclined to do anything with it, or are gaslit into believing they require permission to use their considerable privileges. (The latter point drives me absolutely bananas. What’s the point of being a senator if you have to ask Mother May I every single time you want to BE A SENATOR. No wonder they’re all leaving for different jobs.)

3) The Senate has completely atrophied as a problem solving institution. Usually when things get stuck there are bipartisan “gangs” that form to solve the issue, lead negotiations, or walk the Senate back from the brink. This doesn’t happen anymore largely because senators don’t feel they have individual agency. See points 1 and 2. 

4) Also per the last point, the committees are too large, and senators are on too many, to allow them to focus on two or three things and become The Guy about That Thing. 

5) The committees are also deferential to leadership in a way they didn’t used to be, and that lack of independence dulls vital skill sets because it relies on other people to chew your food for you.

6) The modern Senate will do nothing unless they have a predetermined outcome. How many times has “we don’t have 60” been used as an excuse to do nothing? The Senate is a majestic institution precisely BECAUSE it is designed to leverage uncertainty into consensus. You never know how things will actually end until you fight them to the floor and give issues a political process, force a negotiation, and don’t give up until you’ve come to a solution. The greatest causes in American history didn’t *begin* with 60 or 67 (former cloture threshold) votes. They ended there after massive exertion and process. Modern Senates refuse to countenance a) the workload required and b) the uncertainty of the outcome.

Almost every CFD prop firm seems to be exploring or launching a Perpetual Futures model. But here's a question worth asking:

Why aren't these firms bringing the same model to CFD trading with MT5?

They already have the infrastructure, technology, liquidity providers, and experience in the CFD industry. So why not introduce more flexible, trader-friendly CFD models instead of following the same trend?

Perpetual Futures may be gaining popularity, but CFD traders still represent a massive market. MT5 remains a familiar and preferred platform for many traders.

Innovation shouldn't mean simply copying the latest business model. It should mean giving traders more choices, better trading conditions, transparent rules, and a sustainable environment.

Why not innovate in the market you already dominate rather than chasing the next trend?
